item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dodgers vs Brewers NLCS: Series Preview and Injury Report
item.dc:creator: Cody Snavely

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE, WI—The Los Angeles Dodgers and Milwaukee Brewers are set to renew their postseason rivalry in the National League Championship Series, meeting for the second consecutive year and third time since 2018. While Milwaukee dominated the regular-season series, Los Angeles has owned this matchup in October, sweeping the Brewers in the 2025 NLCS and eliminating them in seven games in 2018.
The Dodgers also swept Milwaukee in the 2020 Wild Card Series, giving them a perfect record in three postseason meetings. Los Angeles has reached the World Series every time it has faced the Brewers in October, winning two of those three trips. Milwaukee will look to change that history after earning home-field advantage with a 103-win regular season.
The clubs met seven times during the 2026 regular season, with the Brewers winning four games and the Dodgers taking three. Despite losing the season series, Los Angeles outscored Milwaukee 27-25, setting the stage for another competitive October matchup.
The first meeting came from May 22nd through May 24th in Milwaukee, where the Dodgers won two of three. After dropping the opener, 5-1, Los Angeles bounced back with an 11-3 victory behind Teoscar Hernández, who hit a three-run homer and drove in six runs. Yoshinobu Yamamoto then delivered seven innings of one-run ball in the series finale, while Andy Pages homered in a 5-1 Dodgers win.
Milwaukee responded when the teams met again at Dodger Stadium from August 13th through August 16th, winning three of four games. The Brewers rallied against Edwin Díaz in the ninth inning to take the opener, wasting a strong start from Roki Sasaki. The Dodgers evened the series the following day behind another quality outing from Yamamoto, with Pages and Tommy Edman homering in a 3-1 victory.
The Brewers took control from there, beating Los Angeles 4-1 behind six strong innings from Jacob Misiorowski before closing out the series with a 6-2 win. Logan Henderson held the Dodgers to one run over seven innings in the finale, while Milwaukee capitalized on defensive mistakes and bullpen struggles to secure the season-series victory.
Despite those results, the Dodgers enter the NLCS with reasons for optimism, particularly after hitting eight home runs against Atlanta in the NLDS. Max Muncy led the way with three, while Freddie Freeman added two as Los Angeles rediscovered its power after a quieter second half. Milwaukee, meanwhile, relies less on the long ball and more on a deep lineup that led the majors with a .258 batting average, .341 on-base percentage and 10.6% walk rate.
The pitching matchup could ultimately decide the series. Los Angeles boasts a formidable rotation led by Tarik Skubal and Yamamoto, both of whom delivered dominant starts against Atlanta. Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow add depth, giving the Dodgers an advantage in established starting pitching. Milwaukee counters with Jacob Misiorowski, who posted a 1.80 ERA and 252 strikeouts during the regular season, but questions remain about his role in the rotation.
The Brewers have the edge in the bullpen, however, after posting the National League’s best relief ERA at 3.40. Closer Trevor Megill converted 30 of 33 save opportunities, while Abner Uribe and Milwaukee’s collection of left-handed relievers give manager Pat Murphy several reliable late-inning options. The Dodgers’ bullpen looked sharper in the NLDS, but sustaining that success against Milwaukee will be essential.
Milwaukee also has defensive and baserunning advantages, ranking among the league’s best in defensive runs saved and stealing 162 bases during the regular season. The Dodgers’ defensive lapses against Atlanta showed how costly mistakes can become in October, making execution especially important against a Brewers team that thrives on putting pressure on its opponents.
Still, Los Angeles has the postseason experience and star power to make another deep run. Dave Roberts continues to prove he can navigate October, and the Dodgers have repeatedly delivered in high-pressure moments against Milwaukee. The Brewers’ 103 wins and regular-season success make them a formidable opponent. Still, the Dodgers’ rotation, power potential, and postseason pedigree give them a path to a third consecutive NLCS victory.
The regular-season results suggest this rematch could be tightly contested. If Los Angeles gets length from its starters, capitalizes on scoring opportunities, and limits defensive mistakes, it has a strong chance to continue its October dominance over Milwaukee. The Brewers, meanwhile, will look to use their bullpen depth, athletic defense, and relentless offense to turn the rivalry in their favor finally.
Pitching Matchup
Game One: Tarik Skubal (LHP) (1-0, 1.50 ERA) vs. Jacob Misiorowski (0-0, 4.50 ERA)
Game Two: Yoshinobu Yamamoto (1-0, 1.29 ERA) vs. TBD (0-0, 0.00 ERA)

Who’s In & Who’s Out?
The Dodgers enter their National League Championship Series rematch against the Brewers with several injury concerns, headlined by infielder Miguel Rojas, whose availability remains uncertain as the team finalizes its postseason roster.
Rojas is dealing with lower left back and hip pain and remains day-to-day. He completed an “encouraging” workout on October 9th, according to manager Dave Roberts. However, the Dodgers are still determining whether the veteran infielder is healthy enough to make the NLCS roster. Given his postseason experience and defensive versatility, Rojas’ status will be one of the biggest decisions facing Los Angeles ahead of the series.
On the pitching side, right-hander Will Klein could provide a potential reinforcement if the Dodgers need additional bullpen depth. Klein has been sidelined with right elbow discomfort since landing on the injured list on August 1st before being transferred to the 60-day injured list on September 2nd. He has progressed to facing hitters and remains a possible option for the postseason.
However, the Dodgers are unlikely to have right-hander Blake Treinen available for the NLCS. Treinen suffered right shoulder inflammation while warming up in the bullpen on September 26th and was placed on the 15-day injured list the following day. Although baseball operations president Andrew Friedman has not completely ruled out a postseason return, Treinen is expected to miss the rest of the 2026 campaign, with a return more likely in 2027.
Beyond those immediate postseason concerns, Los Angeles has several pitchers whose recoveries are expected to extend into next season. Right-hander Gavin Stone, who is dealing with right shoulder inflammation, was placed on the injured list on March 22nd and transferred to the 60-day injured list on April 1st. He finished the Triple-A season on a rehab assignment with Oklahoma City and is expected to return in 2027.
Right-hander Jake Cousins is also targeting a 2027 return as he continues recovering from Tommy John surgery. He was placed on the injured list on March 24th and transferred to the 60-day injured list on April 1st, finishing the Triple-A season on a rehab assignment with Oklahoma City. Similarly, right-hander Ben Casparius remains sidelined with right shoulder inflammation after landing on the injured list on April 13th and being transferred to the 60-day injured list on May 18th. He also finished the Triple-A season on a rehab assignment and is expected to return in 2027.
The Dodgers’ remaining injured pitchers face longer-term recovery timelines as well. Left-hander Eric Lauer was placed on the 15-day injured list on September 2nd with left elbow inflammation before being transferred to the 60-day injured list on September 11th. He is ineligible to return before the end of the season and is expected to remain out until 2027.
Right-hander Brusdar Graterol’s timeline is less certain. Recovering from right shoulder and lower back surgeries, Graterol was placed on the injured list on March 22nd and transferred to the 60-day injured list on May 17th. He later shared on social media that he underwent a surgical procedure on his back, and no timetable has been established for his return.
Day-to-day (1): Miguel Rojas
10-day Injured List (0):
15-day Injured List (1): Blake Treinen
60-day Injured List (6): Jake Cousins, Gavin Stone, Ben Casparius, Brusdar Graterol, Will Klein, Eric Lauer
The Brewers will enter their National League Championship Series rematch against the Dodgers dealing with several injuries, including multiple pitchers who will miss the remainder of the 2026 season. While most of the club’s injured players are expected to return in 2027, right-hander Brandon Woodruff remains a potential option if Milwaukee makes a deep postseason run.
Woodruff has been sidelined since being placed on the 60-day injured list on July 5th, with his designation transferred on July 12th, due to a right shoulder capsule injury. The veteran right-hander was recently cleared by his shoulder surgeon to attempt throwing off a mound, leaving open the possibility of a return during the World Series. However, time is running short for him to work his way back into game shape. “I know the clock is ticking against me,” Woodruff said on October 3rd. “But I’m trying, that’s for sure.”
Milwaukee’s No. 2 prospect, infielder Luis Peña, is expected to miss the remainder of the 2026 season and much of 2027 after fracturing his left fibula while stealing third base on September 5th. He was placed on the minor league seven-day injured list on September 6th and underwent surgery on September 24th. With a typical recovery timeline of six to nine months, Peña is expected to return in 2027.
Left-hander Brian Fitzpatrick has been out since being placed on the 60-day injured list on June 6th, with his designation transferred on June 9th, due to a left UCL strain. After seeking a second opinion from Dr. Keith Meister, Fitzpatrick underwent Tommy John surgery on July 1st. He is expected to miss the rest of the 2026 season and is not projected to return until mid or late 2027.
Right-hander Quinn Priester was placed on the injured list on March 25th and transferred to the 60-day injured list on June 6th after being diagnosed with right neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome. He underwent successful season-ending thoracic outlet decompression surgery in Dallas on June 22nd and is expected to be ready for the start of the 2027 season.
Left-hander Angel Zerpa has been sidelined since April 29th due to left forearm tightness. He was transferred to the 60-day injured list on May 31st and underwent season-ending Tommy John surgery in Dallas on May 11th. Zerpa is expected to miss the remainder of the 2026 season, with a potential return projected for early to mid-2027.

10-day Injured List (00):

item.content:encoded:
Pete Crow-Armstrong could end up winning the MVP, but he may not be able to escape the criticism that comes with a lackluster display in the postseason. The Cubs, who looked like a World Series contender in the regular season, were swept by the San Diego Padres in the Wild Card round. Crow-Armstrong went 0-for-7 with one walk and four strikeouts against the Padres. As a result, the Cubs scored just one run across the two-game series, losing 8-0 in Game 1 and 4-1 in Game 2.
On Friday, MLB analyst Dan Clark blamed PCA for coming up short in the postseason, especially after finishing the regular season with 45 home runs, 41 stolen bases, 107 RBIs and 119 runs scored. He added that the postseason slump could overshadow his regular season heroics.
"Pete Crow-Armstrong's horrendous Postseason has escaped criticism," Clark wrote on X.
"His poorly-timed slump was one of the main reasons the overrated Cubs were swept aside so easily. He might win the MVP Award, but his strong regular season will forever be remembered for his Postseason choke."
However, it would be unfair to put the blame entirely on PCA for the Cubs' offensive slump. Alex Bregman also went hitless, and the two hitters combined for eight strikeouts. The Padres' pitchers also deserved the credit for keeping the Cubs hitters from doing any damage.
Pete Crow-Armstrong Takes Ownership for Cubs Postseason Exit
Instead of blaming the Padres' pitching staff's solid execution, Pete Crow-Armstrong held himself responsible for a poor showing at the plate. PCA looked down upon himself with disappointment after the Cubs were eliminated in the Wild Card round.
"I would say, to start: I show up. I show up when it matters in these games. That would help us immediately. But that's all I got right now," PCA said. "You can look at the scoreboard, you can look at the stat sheet, wherever you get your numbers from, and it is clear to see that I didn't contribute… None of it feels good. Pretty disappointed in myself, but that's for me to work on."
PCA's solid regular season, where he became just the seventh player in MLB history to join the 40-40 club, was the primary reason behind the Cubs' postseason qualification. The Cubs centerfielder has overtaken Shohei Ohtani as the leading NL MVP candidate after contrasting ends to seasons for both of them.

item.content:encoded:
Misiorowski will start Game 1 of the NLCS against the Dodgers on Sunday.
Misiorowski took the mound to begin the opening contest of the NLDS against San Diego, and the Brewers will turn to their ace again to begin their best-of-seven series against Los Angeles. The 24-year-old is a strong contender to take home the NL Cy Young Award after posting a 1.80 ERA and 0.80 WHIP across 174.2 innings in the regular season, but he wasn't quite as dominant during his first postseason outing, allowing two runs on four hits and a walk while fanning six batters in four innings.

item.content:encoded:
Baseball postseason, for all of its unpredictability, has brought us the meeting of the two best teams in the sport to determine the National League representative in the World Series. Ahead of last season's NLCS, the angle of David versus Goliath was heavily played in virtually any analysis—it didn't help the more centered angle that the Dodgers steamrolled the Brewers on their way to a sweep. This time around it might not be that simple.
The similarities are evident, with the Brewers, yet again, having home-field advantage as a team that better maximized its skill set in the regular season, all while the Dodgers remain the favorites to advance, as was the case last season. Having said that, foolish are those who project a similar imbalance to that of the previous NLCS—the expectation of a more tightly contested series goes through pitching.
It may appear like a small factor, but the fact that both teams won their Division Series in four games means that Pat Murphy and Dave Roberts can line up their pitching in the ideal way for this Championship Series. And pitching is the great equalizer here, as both teams are stacked in that department and neither offense is currently hot enough to the point of putting into question the likelihood of a series dominated by elite pitching.
For all the talent on the mound for the Dodgers, the odds-on favorite to win the NL Cy Young pitches on the other side in Jacob Misiorowski. He is joined by the rookie Logan Henderson at the front end of a pitching staff tied with the Dodgers for the second-highest ERA+ in baseball. Last year's Brewers ace, Freddy Peralta, was good, not great, in the series against Los Angeles, and that applied to several key Brewers pitchers in order for the Dodgers to sweep the series in four without major offensive explosions.
With starting pitching on both sides able to dominate, the Dodgers have an advantage from last season's team in that the bullpen brings a much greater sense of reliability, not only in depth but also in the backend. We probably get the sense most fans will watch Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott, waiting for them to fail all the way until the hypothetical final out of the World Series—but they've done enough to earn Dave Roberts' trust, and the plethora of options behind them ready for a high-leverage spot if things go south isn't to be ignored.
Such emphasis on pitching is a must from the Brewers side because offensively, despite Jake Bauers' breakout campaign at first, the Dodgers still retain a heavy advantage, one that might even be currently underplayed ahead of the series. With little to no action from some of its top hitters, the Dodgers weren't brilliant, but they still got theirs in key spots against the feisty Braves. Last postseason, the Dodgers offense wasn't bombastic against Milwaukee, but it did enough to capitalize on strong pitching, while the Brewers' attack was nowhere to be found against elite Dodger starting pitching.
Second to last in regular-season homers and top five in stolen bases, the Brewers' offense's best course of action to put a dent in Dodger pitching is through generating action on the basepaths — putting the bat on the ball and pressuring a defense that has vulnerabilities (I won't name any names — Teoscar Hernández, cough, cough). It's nearly unfathomable to imagine Blake Snell or Tyler Glasnow escaping a five-walk outing with just one run against the Brewers like they did facing the Braves.
All season long, the National League has clearly proven to be the superior league. It's only fitting that the winner of the NLCS, whoever that is, will enter the Fall Classic as the favorite to win it all — the Dodgers in pursuit of a threepeat and the Brewers in search of their first title.

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers make Tarik Skubal decision that should worry Brewers before NLCS showdown originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Los Angeles Dodgers are four victories away from returning to the World Series, and manager Dave Roberts has revealed how his team plans to attack the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series.
Roberts announced Friday that Tarik Skubal will start Game 1 on Sunday, with Yoshinobu Yamamoto scheduled to pitch Game 2 on Monday. The decision gives Los Angeles two of baseball's most accomplished pitchers to begin a series that features the National League's top two regular-season teams.
The announcement also provides another reminder of the extraordinary pitching depth the Dodgers have assembled. Los Angeles is attempting to win its third consecutive World Series championship, and its starting rotation could become the biggest obstacle standing between Milwaukee and its own championship ambitions.
Tarik Skubal gets another opportunity to set the tone
Skubal will take the mound Sunday at American Family Field after delivering an excellent performance against the Atlanta Braves in the Division Series. The two-time Cy Young Award winner allowed one run on two hits over six innings in Game 1, striking out seven batters while issuing two walks.
Tarik Skubal will start Game 1 with Yoshinobu Yamamoto starting Game 2 for the Dodgers in the NLCS against the Brewers, per @ByJackHarris https://t.co/e8wI91D6uF
— Talkin' Baseball (@TalkinBaseball_) October 9, 2026
Los Angeles acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers in a blockbuster August trade, adding another established ace to an already talented pitching staff. His arrival strengthened a rotation that included Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, giving Roberts multiple options capable of controlling a postseason game.
Starting Skubal in Game 1 is an important decision because Milwaukee owns home-field advantage in the series. The Brewers finished the regular season with 103 victories, while the Dodgers reached the 100-win mark. A strong opening performance would allow Los Angeles to immediately put pressure on a team that has been extremely difficult to beat throughout the year.
Skubal's ability to limit baserunners and generate strikeouts could be particularly valuable against a Milwaukee lineup featuring Christian Yelich, Jackson Chourio and William Contreras.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto gives Dodgers another major advantage
Yamamoto will follow Skubal in Game 2 after producing one of the Dodgers' best pitching performances against Atlanta. The right-hander struck out 10 batters over seven innings, allowing only one run on four hits in a victory that helped Los Angeles regain control of the Division Series.
The performance continued an impressive postseason history for Yamamoto, who earned World Series MVP honors in 2025. His ability to deliver deep, efficient outings gives Roberts another dependable option before the series shifts to Dodger Stadium. Milwaukee is expected to rely heavily on its own talented young pitchers, including Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson. The Brewers have demonstrated throughout the season that they can compete with baseball's most talented rosters, but matching Los Angeles on the mound will be a significant challenge.
The Dodgers also have decisions remaining beyond their first two starters. Roberts indicated Friday that the team was considering adding another pitcher to its NLCS roster, a move that would require removing a position player.
Dodgers still have questions despite pitching advantage
One concern involves veteran utility player Miguel Rojas, who left Game 3 against Atlanta because of lower back discomfort. Rojas participated in baseball activities Friday, but Roberts stopped short of confirming his availability for the championship series.
The Dodgers eliminated Atlanta in four games, while Milwaukee also advanced with a four-game victory over San Diego. The teams now meet in the NLCS for the second consecutive postseason, creating another opportunity for the Brewers to challenge the defending champions. Game 1 is scheduled for Sunday at 8 p.m. ET, with Game 2 following Monday at 5 p.m. ET.
Los Angeles has plenty of offensive talent, including Shohei Ohtani, but its starting pitching could determine how this series unfolds. By sending Skubal and Yamamoto to the mound in Milwaukee, Roberts is giving the Dodgers an opportunity to establish control before returning home.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- The Dodgers' elite starting pitching was the driving force when they successfully defended their World Series title in 2025. As the back-to-back champions bid for a three-peat, their four-headed monster of a rotation has already been just as impactful four games into their postseason.
Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tyler Glasnow recorded a combined 1.69 ERA (four earned runs in 21 1/3 innings) in four games in the NL Division Series against the Braves, the second-lowest mark among this year's postseason rotations. The Rays' starters hold a slight edge with a 1.65 ERA (three earned runs in 16 1/3 innings) in three games.
"To see it play out in the way it did was not surprising," president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said. "But just the way they went out and competed, the way they challenged each other, we're excited for this next round and for them to get us deep into games and be a huge part of us, hopefully, winning eight more games."
As the second seed in the NL field, the Dodgers had a bye week and were able to reset their rotation to their liking for the postseason. Because they won the NLDS in four games, they'll be able to tweak their starting four again ahead of their NL Championship Series against the Brewers, which begins on Sunday at American Family Field.
With manager Dave Roberts announcing on Friday that Skubal will start Game 1 and Yamamoto Game 2, here's how the Dodgers' rotation could look through the first four games:
Skubal would have started a winner-take-all Game 5 against the Braves on Friday, but the Dodgers took care of business in four. So they'll send their big Trade Deadline reinforcement to the hill for the NLCS opener against the Brewers, who were among the other teams interested in acquiring him this summer.
Milwaukee also has yet to officially announce its rotation order, but Jacob Misiorowski appears lined up to start opposite Skubal, setting up a must-see matchup between the back-to-back AL Cy Young Award winner and this year's presumptive NL Cy Young Award winner.
The Dodgers raised eyebrows by waiting until Game 3 to start Yamamoto in the NLDS. They actually made that decision with the NLCS in mind, as Yamamoto will likely jump ahead of Snell to start Game 2 on his usual five days' rest. Yamamoto would then be available to start a potential Game 6 on his normal rest as well.
Yamamoto has never started on fewer than five days' rest with the Dodgers, but he won last year's World Series MVP honors after closing out Game 7 on zero days' rest. The right-hander said he would be open to pitching on shorter rest and/or in relief again this postseason, but L.A. will try to keep him working on his typical rest unless the situation necessitates it.
Snell showed some rust when he started NLDS Game 2, which was just his third appearance in the span of 2 1/2 weeks because of left groin tightness that flared up in mid-September. He would be working on extended rest if the Dodgers push him to Game 3, but having some more time to fine-tune his delivery might be helpful given how little he has pitched recently.
Remarkably, the Dodgers are 7-0 when Glasnow pitches in a postseason game for them. That Glasnow is the No. 4 starter in this rotation speaks to the depth of the group, as he could be the ace on many other staffs around the Majors.

item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND -- This must be how it had to be.
The White Sox and Guardians have exhausted each other all year. They played 13 times in the regular season, with seven games decided by one run and four ending with a walk-off. Their AL Central battle came down to a single game. And now, their best-of-five ALDS has reached a decisive Game 5 on Saturday night, at what will be a packed and passionate Progressive Field.
These teams’ scouting reports on each other are so detailed at this point that they include players’ childhood fears and preferred orders at the airport Cinnabon. There are old married couples that haven’t spent as much time together as the 2026 Sox and Guardians.
But only one of them can advance to face the No. 1-seeded Rays in the ALCS, which begins Monday at Tropicana Field. And with both Chicago and Cleveland having won two games apiece in the other’s domain, this deeply personal hard-fought series -- the only LDS to go the distance this year -- will now get the winner-take-all it deserves.
“Just on to the next,” White Sox shortstop Colson Montgomery said. “Flush these last two games. It’s out of our control now. All we can control is how we show up on Saturday.”
After Gavin Williams closed out the Guardians’ win in Game 4 with an emergency relief appearance, he will take the ball in Game 5 for his second start this series. Williams, who struck out an AL-best 248 batters in the regular season, struck out 11 more in only five innings in Game 2.
“It's a Game 5, win or go home,” manager Stephen Vogt said. “Gavin wants the ball. We want him to have the ball, and it's his game.”
Give Cleveland credit for pulling itself off the mat in a tough environment on the South Side. José Ramírez roared to life, and a Guards offense that had been flat in Games 1 and 2 scored 18 runs total across Games 3 and 4.
The last team to rally from an 0-2 hole in a best-of-five series and win it was the 2017 Yankees … against Cleveland. The Guardians could join the 2001 Yankees (vs. A’s), 2012 Giants (vs. Reds) and 2015 Blue Jays (vs. Rangers) as the only teams to come back from 0-2 in the Division Series after losing the first two at home. One figures that if the Guardians are going to end the longest active championship drought in the sport (dating back to 1948), they might as well do it the hard way.
“I think momentum's definitely going be big in this next one,” Steven Kwan said. “We kind of let the home crowd down those first two games. So hopefully it's another chance at redemption.”
As for the Sox, they missed their chance to clinch a playoff series at home for the first time since 1906. But that trivia is trivial compared to the ultimate goal of reaching the next round in any way, shape or form. No one expected Chicago to even reach the playoffs this year, but this No. 6-seeded team has made serious noise with its unorthodox pitching plan. And as bad as things went at home, at least they come into Game 5 with their best starter, Sean Burke, rested and ready.
“Play our baseball,” White Sox second baseman Chase Meidroth said. “Some at-bats we bounced back and had some good little runs. Couldn’t get that big hit. But they are a good staff and a great pitching staff. It’s not easy, it’s not easy against them ever.”
This exhausting, exhilarating AL Central rivalry has one game left to play. It’s the Central focus of the baseball world.
When is the game and how can I tune in?
Game 5 of the ALDS presented by Booking.com is scheduled for Saturday at 8 ET/7 CT on TBS/truTV/UniMas/HBO Max.
The ALDS will be available in Spanish on UniMas, while Univision’s TUDN Radio will provide Spanish-language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB Postseason games.
Who are the starting pitchers?
White Sox manager Will Venable committed to Burke starting Game 5 during a Friday afternoon Zoom session from Rate Field. The right-hander had a 2-0 record with a 1.04 ERA in three regular-season appearances (two starts) against the Guardians, so the White Sox have to feel confident.
Key stat: Williams is coming off his first relief appearance at any level as a professional. Before that, his previous bullpen experience came in 2021 while in college at East Carolina.
The Guardians’ advantage in earning a postseason first-round bye was their ability to get Parker Messick and Williams two starts apiece in the ALDS. Ironically, Messick’s 2 1/3-inning effort in Game 4 prompted an unplanned bullpen game in which Cleveland used seven additional pitchers -- including Williams, who got the final three outs.
Vogt on Friday announced Williams, who threw 18 pitches, will be his Game 5 starter.
“After the game last night, I was walking by his office and I told him I was ready to go,” Williams said Friday. “Whatever [I need to do] to help the team win, that's what I'm going to do. It doesn't matter the role at this point.”
What do the starting lineups look like?
White Sox: With the right-handed throwing power of Williams potentially on the mound, look for Venable to go back to his left-handed directed lineup.
Guardians: Patrick Bailey figures to be back behind the plate after he went 2-for-3 with a pinch-hit home run and two RBIs in Game 4. It will be curious if the Guardians make a switch in the outfield, given Angel Martínez is 0-for-15 with eight strikeouts this series. Daniel Schneemann, Petey Halpin and David Fry each are options on the ALDS roster.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
White Sox: Grant Taylor explained after Thursday’s rough showing (where he faced six hitters and didn’t retire any of them) how he will be ready to throw Saturday in any form even if it’s nine innings. The White Sox will be using whomever they have available, whether it’s relievers or starters, to get through Game 5.
Guardians: Whoever advances to the ALCS will do so with a pitching staff that has carried a heavy workload this series. The Guardians will worry about Game 1 of that series if they are fortunate to get there, Vogt said Thursday night. It will be all hands on deck coming out of the off-day on Friday.
“Obviously we need to see how everybody feels today,” Vogt said Friday. “We need to see how everybody feels coming in tomorrow. But I think if you're a pitcher on our roster, be ready to go tomorrow.”
Any injuries of note?
White Sox: None.
Guardians: Austin Hedges took a Teel foul tip off his right knee in the second inning in Game 4. He was sore on Friday, Vogt said, but the skipper expressed optimism Hedges will be ready to go on Saturday.
Who is hot and who is not?
White Sox: Miguel Vargas homered in the ninth inning off Cade Smith Thursday and reached base three other times via the walk. Munetaka Murakami singled while also walking twice.
Anything else fans might want to know?
- Vargas has reached base 12 times in total during the series.
- Bailey’s pinch-hit homer in the fifth inning of Game 4 was the first by the Guardians in the postseason since Jhonkensy Noel in Game 3 of the 2024 ALCS.

item.dc:creator: David Venn

In that tournament, Caminero tied for the overall lead in home runs with three and slashed .35
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG – As he waited in the on-deck circle before an at-bat last Saturday in Game 1 of the American League Division Series, with more than 40,000 vociferous Rays and Yankees fans in attendance at Tropicana Field, Tampa Bay third baseman Junior Caminero remarked to manager Kevin Cash that he hadn't seen an atmosphere like that since the World Baseball Classic in March at Miami’s loanDepot park.
In that tournament, Caminero tied for the overall lead in home runs with three and slashed .350/.409/.850 for the Dominican Republic in six games. This month, after coming into this postseason with just two playoff at-bats under his belt as a rookie in the 2023 AL Wild Card Series against the Rangers, Caminero is 3-for-10 with a double and two runs scored, helping the Rays sweep the Yankees in the ALDS.
Another member of the Rays who stood out in the World Baseball Classic has also had a solid start to this year’s postseason for Tampa Bay. That would be Jonathan Aranda, who had had just one postseason at-bat in his career before this season – also in '23 against Texas.
After slashing .357/.438/.643 with a home run for Team Mexico in four games at Houston’s Daikin Park in March, the Rays' first baseman came up big in the ALDS, producing the only run in Game 1 with a 417-foot round-tripper off Gerrit Cole and posting a .333/.385/.583 for the series, including an RBI single in Wednesday’s clinching victory.
Seeing Caminero and Aranda have that type of success in their first prolonged Major League postseason, Cash sees a correlation between their exposure to the atmosphere of the WBC and what they’re experiencing now in the postseason.
“I go back to the WBC,” Cash said. “If you ask those two individuals you’re talking about, I think they would say that that environment in the WBC is as intense as any environment that they’ve witnessed in their careers.
“We know that both of those guys really took off for their countries; whether it was the Dominican Republic or Team Mexico, they were huge parts of their success. The big at-bats, the big hits, I think it really helped them. And more than anything, they were excited to get the opportunity to do this now in Major League playoff baseball.”
In Miami’s Pool D, the atmosphere was electric, with the Dominican Republic and eventual tournament champion Venezuela among the countries playing in front of passionate sellout crowds cheering on their nations’ teams. And in Houston’s Pool B, Mexico also had large partisan crowds rooting for the bordering nation, an environment crescendoed with the matchup against the United States in pool play.
“I don’t think you can say the moment’s been too big for either of them,” Cash said, once again crediting their experiences in the Classic as part of their overall preparedness for the MLB postseason. “I think they had really good, strong series in the DS. I think those two guys have had tremendous at-bats for us.”

item.title: [SportsTalk ATL] Former MLB GM believes Braves should target Randy Arozarena - SportsTalk ATL
item.dc:creator: SportsTalk ATL; Chase Irle
item.description: After another underwhelming postseason, a significant chunk of Braves Country is ready for sweeping changes to the team’s core. Maybe this is the year it finally happens. But more than likely, Alex Anthopoulos will be staring down the same two holes in the lineup that have haunted Atlanta for half a decade. item.content:encoded:
After another underwhelming postseason, a significant chunk of Braves Country is ready for sweeping changes to the team’s core. Maybe this is the year it finally happens. But more than likely, Alex Anthopoulos will be staring down the same two holes in the lineup that have haunted Atlanta for half a decade.
The Braves haven’t had a legitimate shortstop since Dansby Swanson walked in free agency after the 2022 season. Orlando Arcia gave them one good half and then cratered. Nick Allen was a glove and nothing else. And Ha-Seong Kim might go down as one of the worst free agent signings in franchise history — which is almost impressive, considering it was only a one-year deal.
The trouble with finding a replacement is simple: shortstops cost a fortune, and nobody trades a good one once they have him. So Atlanta has been left scraping the bottom of the barrel. But the Braves actually have a solution sitting right in front of them in Mauricio Dubon. He’s an elite defender who was more than adequate at the plate, and bringing him back on a two- or three-year deal — a bridge until one of their prospect shortstops is ready — makes all the sense in the world.
That leaves left field as the one spot where Atlanta can upgrade on offense. And if there’s a blemish on Anthopoulos’ résumé, it’s how he’s handled this position since 2021. Jarred Kelenic was a horrendous whiff. Jurickson Profar was somehow worse. Mike Yastrzemski was just average this past season. Left field is where teams get to hide a shaky defender in exchange for offense — and the Braves have gotten next to nothing out of it since their World Series run.
That has to change in 2027, and making it happen will require Anthopoulos to write a bigger check. Former MLB GM Steve Phillips thinks he knows the perfect target: Randy Arozarena.
@StevePhillipsGM believes Randy Arozarena could be a fit for the Braves this offseason in free agency — should Atlanta make him the answer to its left field void? 👀 pic.twitter.com/Dt8KNKB5Vl
— 680 The Fan (@680TheFan) October 8, 2026
The version of Arozarena we saw in Seattle this year would fit any team in need of a left fielder. He posted 5.7 WAR, hitting 26 home runs with an .865 OPS — and arguably the two best seasons of his career have come in his last two with the Mariners, earning All-Star honors both times.
He’s also built for October. Over 45 career postseason games, Arozarena is hitting .292 with a .946 OPS, and the fact that he isn’t a home-run-or-bust bat should be especially enticing for a Braves lineup starving for guys who hit for average and get on base.
It’s a match made in heaven — but the price and the age could force Atlanta to pivot. Arozarena will be looking for at least a three-year deal this offseason, and probably could land four after the year he just had. Set to turn 32 next season, that’s a hefty commitment for a player who could fade early into the contract. That’s exactly the kind of risk the Braves have historically avoided, and as much as I love the fit, I’m skeptical they’ll do what it takes to get it done.
—
Photo: IMAGO / ZUMA Press Wire

item.title: [The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette] José Ramírez homers as the Guardians beat the White Sox 9-5 to force a decisive Game 5 in ALDS | Arkansas Democrat Gazette
item.dc:creator: JAY COHEN AP Baseball Writer
item.description: CHICAGO -- Jose Ramirez homered and drove in three runs, and the Cleveland Guardians beat the Chicago White Sox 9-5 on Thursday night to send their American League division series to a winner-takes-all Game 5. Pinch-hitter Patrick Bailey also went deep as the Guardians won for the second consecutive day after beginning their postseason with two straight losses at home. item.content:encoded:
CHICAGO -- Jose Ramirez homered and drove in three runs, and the Cleveland Guardians beat the Chicago White Sox 9-5 on Thursday night to send their American League division series to a winner-takes-all Game 5.
Pinch-hitter Patrick Bailey also went deep as the Guardians won for the second consecutive day after beginning their postseason with two straight losses at home. Jo Adell hit a two-run single to cap a six-run sixth inning for the AL Central champions.
Cleveland is looking to become the first major league team to come back from a 2-0 deficit in a best-of-five playoff series since the 2017 New York Yankees accomplished the feat against, well, Cleveland. Teams with a 2-0 lead in a best-of-five postseason series have gone on to win 83 of 93 times.
Game 5 is back in Cleveland on Saturday night.
Chicago's bullpen -- one of its biggest strengths in a surprising season -- is suddenly looking very tired. Grant Taylor was hit hard after pitching 5 1/3 scoreless innings over the first two games of the series, allowing four runs and four hits without retiring any of the six batters he faced during Cleveland's rally in the sixth.
Miguel Vargas homered late for the White Sox, who flopped in their second straight bid to clinch a postseason series at home for the first time since the 1906 World Series against the Chicago Cubs. Sam Antonacci drove in two runs.
Game 2 starter Gavin Williams got the last three outs for Cleveland after Vargas began the ninth with his first postseason homer. It was the first career relief appearance for Williams, who could start Game 5 for the Guardians.
Cleveland trailed 2-0 before rallying in the fifth. Bailey led off with a pinch-hit homer, and Steven Kwan chased Erick Fedde with a one-out single.
Jordan Hicks came in and Ramirez drove a 99.9 mph fastball deep to right-center for just his second homer since Sept. 1, a span of 26 games. The seven-time All-Star had surgery after he broke a bone in his left hand on a swing June 13.
It was Ramirez's first postseason homer since 2024 and No. 5 overall. He also starred in Game 3, finishing with two hits and two RBis in Cleveland's 9-3 victory.
Chicago responded with two runs in the bottom half, sending a charge through the crowd of 39,920. Antonacci was hit by a pitch from Tim Herrin with the bases loaded, and Brenton Doyle made it 4-3 with a sacrifice fly. The White Sox had the bases loaded with two down, but rookie Braden Montgomery struck out swinging against Erik Sabrowski.
Antonacci has been plunked 33 times this year, including a franchise-record 29 in the regular season. The rookie became the first player in postseason history to be hit by a pitch with the bases loaded multiple times in a career, after he was also plunked in the same situation in Game 3.
Anthony Kay started the sixth for Chicago, but the left-hander was replaced by Taylor after Travis Bazzana's RBI double tied it at 4-4. Bailey greeted Taylor with a run-scoring single, and Cleveland started to pull away.
Walks by Brayan Rocchio and Kwan loaded the bases for Ramirez, who made it 6-4 with an infield single. Chase DeLauter added another run-scoring single before Adell capped the outburst with a liner to right that drove in Kwan and Ramirez.
Adell hit a three-run triple during Cleveland's Game 3 victory. He has 4 hits, 3 walks and 6 RBI in the series.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees Get Candid Offseason Take on Phillies’ Bryce Harper
item.dc:creator: Eduardo Razo
item.description: The New York Yankees have run it back these last couple of offseasons since reaching the 2024 World Series. New York has made tweaks around the team but has kept its core and key supporting cast members intact. Nonetheless, after a second straight elimination in the ALDS, this time at the hands of the Tampa Bay Rays, is it time for the Yankees to shake up the roster and make a blockbuster move this winter? If New York wants to take advantage of the Aaron Judge window, they need to bring in playe
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have run it back these last couple of offseasons since reaching the 2024 World Series. New York has made tweaks around the team but has kept its core and key supporting cast members intact.
Nonetheless, after a second straight elimination in the ALDS, this time at the hands of the Tampa Bay Rays, is it time for the Yankees to shake up the roster and make a blockbuster move this winter?
If New York wants to take advantage of the Aaron Judge window, they need to bring in players who will make an impact right away, and one of the names who could be available is Bryce Harper.
After falling in the Wild Card Series, the Philadelphia Phillies could look to shake up their roster too. As a result, that's led to speculation surrounding whether Harper could be available this offseason.
Philadelphia Phillies on SI's Nick Ziegler put together three landing spots for Harper and one of them is the New York Yankees.
"After being eliminated by the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS in just three games, a team that figures to be looking to shake things up as well is the Yankees," Ziegler wrote in an Oct. 8 article.
"Despite having Aaron Judge for the last several years, they have been mostly a disappointment when it comes to their play in October. Perhaps pairing Harper and Judge together in the lineup would be what helps get New York back over the top."
Would Bryce Harper Fit In New York's Roster?
Despite being in his mid-30s now, Harper had a batting average of .269 with 155 hits, 29 home runs, 87 RBIs, and 93 runs scored in 162 games, per StatMuse. Harper has played in Washington and found individual success in a market like Philadelphia, which can be rough on a player.
Nonetheless, would he want to play in New York, and would the Yankees want to take on his contract, which would see Harper have a base salary of $26 million in 2027, per Spotrac? Then there's the question of position too and whether he'd be at first base or in the outfield.
"While the positional fit might not be great, the Yankees could surely find a way to pull this off," Ziegler added. "Frustrations are certainly growing for New York, and Judge publicly stated after the loss that he would like for the team to go 'all-in.' Getting Harper would certainly signal the team's desire to win right now."
Yankees Receive Ketel Marte Trade Idea After Elimination
Moreover, that isn't the trade speculation surrounding the Yankees since their elimination. Chris Landers of FanSided floated an intriguing trade idea that would allow New York to land the Diamondbacks' Ketel Marte.
When it comes to what the Yankees could give up for Marte, Landers has New York sending: RHP Will Warren, RHP Elmer Rodriguez, and INF Core Jackson.
"It's hard to gauge exactly what Marte's value would be right now. The D-backs hold almost zero leverage here; then again, they could always just decide to try and make it work with their star, who remains a very good player at a premium position on a reasonable contract," Landers wrote in an Oct. 8 article. "Even with all the extenuating factors, it seems hard to believe Arizona wouldn't be able to get something of real value in return.
"This package would certainly qualify. Warren has settled in as a perfectly respectable No. 4 starter, with real room for growth beyond that. He's cracked 150 innings in each of the last two seasons, and he's under team control through 2030. Rodriguez has lost some of his prospect shine, but he also has No. 3 or 4 upside and is ready to compete for a big-league rotation spot right away."
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Yankees Get Candid Offseason Take on Phillies' Bryce Harper appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] José Ramírez, just in time to save the Guardians' season, has rediscovered his MVP form in ALDS vs. White Sox
item.dc:creator: Russell Dorsey
item.description: CHICAGO — Even in the worst full season of his career, a true superstar can turn it on at any time. José Ramírez is arguably one of the five best players in Major League Baseball. He had a down year by his standards in 2026, but the Cleveland Guardians couldn't have picked a better time for their best player to get hot. With their season on the line in Game 4 of the ALDS against the Chicago White Sox and an opportunity to send the series back to Cleveland for a winner-take-all Game 5, the Guardi
item.content:encoded:
CHICAGO — Even in the worst full season of his career, a true superstar can turn it on at any time.
José Ramírez is arguably one of the five best players in Major League Baseball. He had a down year by his standards in 2026, but the Cleveland Guardians couldn't have picked a better time for their best player to get hot. With their season on the line in Game 4 of the ALDS against the Chicago White Sox and an opportunity to send the series back to Cleveland for a winner-take-all Game 5, the Guardians' superman found his cape.
"That's a future Hall of Famer," outfielder Chase DeLauter said after Cleveland's 9-5 victory on Thursday in Chicago. "It's special."
Through the first two games of the ALDS, Ramírez didn't look like the player Cleveland knows him to be, going 0-for-6 with three strikeouts. His early-series struggles seemingly carried over from the final month of the regular season, which saw him put up a paltry .198/.237/.264 slashline with just one home run.
But Game 3 on Wednesday seemed to have unlocked something for the Guardians' superstar. In that one, Ramírez went 2-for-4 with a double, a triple and a stolen base. He took over the game with his bat, glove and his legs. Then Ramírez had even more in store for Game 4.
Just like in Game 3, the White Sox took the momentum early on Thursday, taking a 2-0 lead into the fifth inning and running Guardians starter Parker Messick out of the game after just 2 1/3 innings. But once catcher Patrick Bailey cut the lead in half with a solo shot, it was time for Ramírez to make his mark on the game.
"It's contagious to the team, like the way he plays the game, the energy, his at-bat quality," second baseman Travis Bazzana said postgame. "I mean, we saw him [in Game 3] manufacture a run by himself. He got on, stole some bases and then scored. So he can make the impact so fast, but he plays with such intention."
Prior to Ramírez's fifth-inning at-bat, it felt like a big swing was coming. He flew out in his first at-bat before a sharp lineout in his second. But he found the barrel on both, with exit velocities of 98.9 mph and 97.5 mph, respectively.
Ramírez made sure the third ball he put in play wouldn't be caught. The Guardians' third baseman launched a two-run blast to put Cleveland ahead 3-2 and injected some much-needed confidence into the visiting dugout.
While he doesn't typically show a lot of emotion, Ramírez was sure to fire up his dugout before rounding the bases.
"It's a special moment when you have that type of energy from the guys," he said postgame. "I had a particular conversation with Messick before that. I told him, 'I'm going to get this turned around for you,' and I was able to execute it. It was really special."
Said manager Stephen Vogt: "It was José Ramírez being José Ramírez in the playoffs. Bring in a fastball, [Jordan] Hicks with a great fastball, and Josy got to it. To step up, say there he goes again. And a big moment for him, big moment for us, and he doesn't show a lot of emotion, but he was pretty excited tonight."
Although Cleveland's lead didn't hold long, with Chicago scoring two more in the bottom of the fifth, Ramírez for the second straight day galvanized the Guardians' offense. That three-run outburst in the fifth inning was just an appetizer. The entreé was a monster, six-run sixth inning that made it 9-4 and broke the game open.
As part of that six-run sixth, Ramírez added an RBI single, giving him back-to-back multi-hit games. Since that 0-for-6 in the first two games of the ALDS, the Cleveland superstar is 4-for-9 in the second pair of games, with a double, a triple, a home run, a walk, a stolen base, four runs scored and five RBI.
"It just starts with him. Whether he's hot, whether he's cold, just having him in the lineup, it's that presence," DeLauter said. "When he comes out firing, has that energy, has cool, big swings like that — it just rallies us together."
The numbers will tell you that Ramírez has not been at his best for much of 2026 — he had surgery on the hamate bone in his left hand in June, after all — but you wouldn't know it by his confidence. The seven-time All-Star might not be tall, but he walks around like he's a giant. And that confidence can be felt by everyone around him.
For the Guardians to fight back from a 2-0 series deficit while in Chicago and get back to Cleveland for a chance to reach the ALCS, they needed the best version of Ramírez to show up. And with not a moment to spare, it appears that he has rediscovered his elite form.
Now Cleveland has an opportunity to become the first team since the 2017 New York Yankees to win three straight games in a best-of-five series after losing the first two. Heading back home with a superstar who has gotten hot, an offense that's rolling and a White Sox team that's on the ropes, the Guardians appear to have all the momentum.
"It's going to be crazy," Ramírez said of what he expects for Game 5. "It's going to be an incredible energy. For us, it's going to be the same mindset: Try to win the game, and enjoy the environment that's going to be at Progressive [Field]."

item.title: [Metro Philadelphia] Should the Phillies sign Randy Arozarena or Seiya Suzuki? - Metro Philadelphia
item.dc:creator: Cory Nidoh

item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies will look to improve a roster that once again dealt with injuries and shortcomings, leading to an early exit in the postseason.
The two corner outfield spots are key areas Dave Dombrowski, Preston Mattingly and the front office will need to focus on, along with the bullpen.
Left field has been a platoon over the last two seasons, while the team has struggled to get typical corner outfield production from a right fielder since Nick Castellanos’ All-Star season in 2023, where he clubbed 29 home runs and drove in a career-best 106 runs.
Since 2021, the Phillies have had 26 different starters in left field, with Brandon Marsh, Kyle Schwarber and Andrew McCutchen getting the majority of the starts during that stretch.
Over in right field, the Phillies also penciled in 26 different names to patrol right field, with Nick Castellanos and Bryce Harper earning the lion's share.
Despite the upcoming free agent pool being quite shallow, Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki are a pair of outfielders on the market that the Phillies should target that could provide stability for multiple seasons.
Entering his age 32 season next year (assuming there is a season), Arozarena could be an intriguing pickup for the Phillies. He was named an All-Star with the Seattle Mariners after slashing .281/.381/.484 with an .865 OPS. He hit 26 home runs and drove in 79 runs.
He posted a 151 wRC+ and 5.7 WAR.
Stacking him up to the hitters in the Phillies’ lineup this season, he would have ranked within the top five in AVG, OBP, SLG, OPS, HR and RBIs.
Arozarena is coming off essentially a career year. His triple slash line numbers represent career highs in a full season for the outfielder, and it could have been an outlier campaign for him.
Nonetheless, even his career numbers at .255/.350/.442 and .792 OPS, along with his ability to hit 20-plus homers in six straight seasons, warrant a phone call from the Phillies, who may need him more than any other team in the league.
He would provide much-needed pop from the right side of the plate, something this lineup has been missing for a few years. This season, the Phillies ranked 22nd in MLB in OPS and 28th in on-base percentage from their right-handed hitters.
He also has more speed on the basepaths than Suzuki, adding some athleticism to a Phillies lineup that can become station-to-station at times.
Defensively, he isn't great, but the Phillies need stabilizing bats in the lineup due to the consistent ebbs and flows this lineup has endured over the course of the last handful of seasons, especially come playoff time.
Perhaps the biggest selling point for Arozerena may not be what he does over 162 games, but what he's already done when the stakes are highest.
His postseason résumé gives him an element Suzuki simply doesn't have at the major league level—a proven ability to become a difference-maker when the calendar flips to October.
Arozarena has plenty of experience playing in big moments. He has played in 45 career postseason games, slashing .292/.380/.565 with a .946 OPS across 184 plate appearances. He also has hit 12 bombs in the playoffs and has a knack for the theatrics.
Bringing him in would more than likely mean Brandon Marsh would be traded. The veteran is not a platoon-type bat and would be an everyday plug-and-play-type offensive piece in the middle of the lineup.
He won't be cheap.
Coming off one of his best seasons offensively, he will more than likely command a contract north of $100 million.
While not young either, the Phillies may not have a choice but to add another player in his 30s into the mix to capitalize on the closing title window.
Suzuki, who will turn 33 late next season, would bring similar traits to the lineup that Arozarena would, but perhaps on a more consistent level.
This season, he slashed .270/.368/.473 with an .841 OPS to go with 26 homers, 86 RBIs and a wRC+ of 134.
His 81 walks and 5.1 wins above replacement were career watermarks. It also marked a fourth consecutive season that he posted an OPS north of .800 and third in the last four years, where it was .840 or better.
The outfielder has been a consistent middle-of-the-order bat during his tenure with the Chicago Cubs.
Since 2023, he has had at least 140 hits, 27 doubles, 20 home runs and 70 RBIs. He would be two seasons removed from his best campaign of his five-year big league career in 2025, where he posted career-best in home runs (32) and RBIs (103).
His 113 career home runs are the third-most home runs in Cubs' history, only behind Kris Bryant (138) and Hall of Famer Ernie Banks (136).
During that same stretch he has averaged 28 homers and 97 RBIs per 162-game season. He also averages 72 walks per season during that span, and his patient approach would go a long way for a Phillies lineup that has repeatedly had chase issues, especially in the postseason when it’s become magnified.
Suzuki owns a slightly better career walk rate (10.9%) compared to Arozarena (9.8%).
He’s also a significantly better defender and made major improvements in that department this season. His 14 defensive runs saved this season were good for 17th-best among all outfielders, as opposed to Arozarena’s -2.
The other caveat with Suzuki is that he would be a different type of signing for the organization.
Philadelphia historically has not ventured into signing top Japanese talent, whether directly from Japan or even once they become assimilated stateside in MLB.
Of course, it’s not easy to break into such a market when there is no prior history. Add the fact that the Los Angeles Dodgers have established themselves as the premier destination for Japanese stars looking to take their talents to the top league in the world; it makes it all that more difficult.
The Phillies recently tried their luck with Koyo Aoyagi, a right-handed pitcher the team signed to a minor league contract before the 2025 season. Aoyagi posted a 7.22 ERA between Double-A and Triple-A and never made it to the big league club.
Other examples include Tadahito Iguchi, who they traded for in 2007 and So Taguchi, who they signed after spending six seasons with St. Louis. Neither was the caliber player Suzuki is and is not a success story that the team could use as a recruiting pitch to some of the top players, like star third baseman Teruaki Sato, who plays for the Hanshin Tigers of the Nippon Professional Baseball League.
General manager Preston Mattingly reportedly took a trip overseas to observe the 27-year-old who could be making his way over to the United States.
The Phillies also shouldn’t just sign Suzuki to say they signed a Japanese talent.
However, the talent is there and Suzuki would stabilize right field, a position that has become a revolving door over the last few seasons.
Like Arozarena, Suzuki would command a multi-year deal northwards of $100 million after he signed a five-year, $85 million deal with the Cubs.
But for a Phillies team that has spent years searching for stability in right field since Bryce Harper moved to first base, Suzuki wouldn't be simply another expensive bat. He'd be a proven middle-of-the-order hitter who gets on base, provides above-average defense, and has demonstrated the kind of year-to-year consistency the position has lacked.
Both players certainly fit the needs of the Phillies and wouldn't be a bad starting point to fix this roster.
