item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers' quest for a three-peat begins in earnest on Saturday with Game 1 of the NLDS, as they seek to become the first time since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees to complete a trilogy of titles.
Up to this point, the path for L.A. hasn't been entirely straightforward. There have been times when the Dodgers have looked a bit rickety, and that's to say nothing about everything happening off the field. They are also arguably the most talented team in the playoffs and are coming off another 100-win season.
No matter how you slice it, this is a club with more than its fair share of questions. Let's get into them, starting with the easier ones.
Who are the Dodgers playing in the NLDS?
The Dodgers will face the NL East champion Atlanta Braves, who defeated the Philadelphia Phillies in a three-game wild-card series. The Dodgers went 1-5 against Atlanta in the regular season, getting outscored 26-15.
The winner of the best-of-five series gets the victor of the other NLDS between the Milwaukee Brewers and San Diego Padres.
When do the Dodgers play?
Here's the full NLDS schedule:
| Game | Date | Time (ET) | Channel | Location |
| 1 | Oct. 3 | 4 p.m. | Fox | L.A. |
| 2 | Oct. 4 | 8 p.m. | FS1 | L.A. |
| 3 | Oct. 6 | 6 p.m. | FS1 | Atlanta |
| 4* | Oct. 7 | 6 p.m. | FS1 | Atlanta |
| 5* | Oct. 9 | 8 p.m. | Fox | L.A. |
*if necessary
What will the Dodgers' postseason lineup be?
The Dodgers finished the season shuffling their lineup depending on the handedness of the opposing starting pitcher, and it stands to reason that they will continue doing so in the postseason.
Here's how they could line up against right-handed pitchers:
- Shohei Ohtani, DH
- Mookie Betts, SS
- Freddie Freeman, 1B
- Will Smith, C
- Kyle Tucker, RF
- Teoscar Hernández, LF
- Max Muncy, 3B
- Andy Pages, CF
- Tommy Edman, 2B
Shohei Ohtani has never hit in a batting order position other than leadoff in his MLB postseason career, but lately he has been hitting second against left-handers while Mookie Betts takes his old position atop the order.
Here's L.A.'s left-handed unit:
- Mookie Betts, SS
- Shohei Ohtani, DH
- Freddie Freeman, 1B
- Will Smith, C
- Teoscar Hernández, LF
- Kyle Tucker, RF
- Andy Pages, CF
- Max Muncy, 3B
- Tommy Edman, 2B
Both of those orders alternate left-right all the way down to Edman, a switch-hitter at the bottom. It's entirely possible the Dodgers go a different route, too.
What will the Dodgers' postseason rotation be?
That's fairly settled. The Dodgers will trot out the quartet of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. The order in which those arms are utilized remains to be seen, though the Dodgers have every reason to maximize innings for Yamamoto after what he did last year.
How has this season gone for the Dodgers?
It has gone well, by the standards of any other team.
By the standards of the Dodgers, well, there are a few dynamics at play. This is a good baseball team. They probably should've been better this season, and not just because they have the largest payroll in history, at a projected $410 million, per Roster Resource.
A two-time World Series champion filled its two biggest roster holes by giving two players, Kyle Tucker and Edwin Díaz, the highest salaries in the history of their positions. Entering the season, the Dodgers were estimated by the usually conservative PECOTA projections from Baseball Prospectus to win 104 games, and that didn't take into account acquiring a two-time reigning Cy Young Award winner in Skubal and more at the MLB trade deadline.
So in that sense, 100 wins is a disappointment. One of the most talented teams in MLB history (on paper at least) had more than its fair share of injuries, underperformances and mistakes. There was a point when the club seemed on the verge of letting the NL West become a race, as the Arizona Diamondbacks halved a division lead from 14 games to seven in the span of about a month between July and August, but then the D-backs got mired in their own slump and the Dodgers got hot again.
Overall, the Dodgers' issues boiled down to an offense that slumped hard in July and August, rough days for starting pitchers who will not be starting games in the playoffs and an epically bad bullpen night here and there. The first of those got better in September, though, which you can read more about here.
There is also the Dodgers' 38-37 record against teams with winning records this season, as their worst stretches of the year coincided with some of their toughest road trips and homestands, and that can leave an impression. Of course, it's a bit silly to worry about a team handling its business against good teams when it's going for a three-peat.
How does this team compare to last year's?
It's easy to remember the 2024 and 2025 Dodgers as juggernauts, but both of those teams had flaws that easily could've been fatal.
The 2024 Dodgers entered the postseason with a three-man rotation of Yamamoto, Walker Buehler and Jack Flaherty, with Clayton Kershaw, Glasnow, Dustin May, Gavin Stone, River Ryan and Emmet Sheehan among the starting pitchers on the injured list.
That team was so desperate for starting pitching help that it went full bullpen game while facing elimination at the hands of the Padres in the NLDS. It was only through the grace of a deep and competent bullpen that L.A. triumphed.
The 2025 team had the opposite problem. No one was doubting a rotation of Yamamoto, Snell, Glasnow and Ohtani, but there were most certainly concerns about a bullpen whose late-inning arms consistently blew games well into September.
Once again, the Dodgers adjusted. With their rotation overflowing, they turned to a number of starting pitchers to fill the gaps. Every single pitcher who appeared in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series started at least nine games for this year's team.
With that in mind, the 2026 Dodgers might be the franchise's most balanced roster to enter the postseason in years, but there is once again a major question.
It's Ohtani. Let's get into that.
How's Shohei Ohtani doing?
Ohtani was the overwhelming NL MVP front-runner for the first half of this season, having begun the year as both a hitter and a pitcher for the first time in his Dodgers career.
Then Ohtani's knee started barking in July, resulting in the team taking him off the mound and giving him a lubricant injection during the All-Star break. He also developed a biceps issue at some point.
Those injuries didn't immediately stop Ohtani from playing. Much like he did in his recovery from internal brace surgery in 2024 and 2025, Ohtani played as the Dodgers' every-day designated hitter while rehabbing. However, the injuries clearly started to affect him in September, and the Dodgers opted to put him on the injured list for the first time in his tenure with the team.
Ohtani returned with five games left in the regular season and went 5-for-21 with 1 walk, 8 strikeouts and one extra-base hit, a double. Those numbers clearly aren't up to his standards, but if there's a reason for optimism, it's that he hit batted balls with exit velocities of 106.8, 106, 103.9 and 103.4 mph. He hadn't hit a ball that hard since August. Of course, the flip side of that optimism is maybe a 100% version of him would've hit them even harder.
Since his return, the Dodgers have insisted that Ohtani is feeling better, with hitting coach Aaron Bates saying Thursday that they had absolutely no concerns. The ship has sailed on Ohtani pitching again this season, though.
It still feels like Ohtani is the single biggest question for the Dodgers entering this postseason, given how long-term his knee issue has been. He at least got plenty of rest between his 15-day IL stint and the five days off between the end of the regular season and the start of the NLDS.
Do the Dodgers have a young, dynamic replacement at DH if Ohtani isn't healthy?
What an oddly specific question. The answer is yes, potentially.
It's not a stretch to say that Josue De Paula was the best hitting prospect in baseball at the time of his promotion to fill Ohtani's roster spot in September. At the time, every other position player in the MLB Pipeline top 10 was a shortstop who could offer significant two-way value, while De Paula will eventually be a bat-first corner outfielder at best and a bat-only first baseman at worst.
The good news is De Paula definitely looked like he belonged in his 11 games with the Dodgers while Ohtani was on the IL, slashing .323/.500/.581 and helping inject life into a previously struggling lineup. He was optioned when Ohtani came back, the timing of which made him available for the start of the NLDS.
In the playoffs, De Paula is likely to be the Dodgers' top left-handed bat off the bench, and he could fit in at designated hitter or corner outfield if someone gets hurt. It seems highly unlikely, however, that the Dodgers will take any plate appearances from Ohtani, barring a significant aggravation of that knee issue.
Are Kyle Tucker and Edwin Díaz still having horrifically bad debut seasons for the Dodgers?
Those two players were the butt of jokes all season after they signed record contracts to join the defending champions, then posted the worst seasons of their careers. However, both offered reason for optimism in September.
Tucker entered the month slashing .228/.326/.357 but finished the season at .262/.354/.536, numbers more in line with what the Dodgers were expecting when they signed him to a four-year, $240 million contract. His six homers in September were double what he had in any other month of the season.
In 2026, Díaz made seven appearances with a 10.50 ERA, spent three months on the injured list due to loose bodies in his elbow, came back for nine more appearances, posted a 12.91 ERA in those, then hit the IL one more time in August due to what was described as neck inflammation.
Then he came back in September and, like Tucker, performed like the player the Dodgers were initially expecting, with nine strikeouts and one hit allowed across five scoreless innings. Díaz no longer has the closer role, but he made as good a case as he could for late-inning work in October.
Tucker and Díaz still finished the year with horrendous numbers, and barring some postseason heroics, that's what most fans will remember. Still, it's important to know that the Dodgers might not treat them in October like their overall numbers would suggest.
How's the rest of the Dodgers' bullpen shaping up?
It's a diverse group. We've already talked about Díaz, who could be anything from middle reliever to closer by the end of the postseason. However, the current closer is Tanner Scott, who played the Díaz role last year as the high-priced reliever who struggled in his first year with the Dodgers.
Scott's second season in L.A. has gone far better. He converted 25 of 29 save attempts with a 2.69 ERA.
As for the other six spots in the bullpen, the contenders are Edgardo Henriquez, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Kris Bubic and Brock Stewart from the normal pot of relievers and Roki Sasaki, Justin Wrobleski and Sheehan as overflow from the rotation.
Henriquez might be the most intriguing name from that group, as the flame-throwing right-hander was great during the regular season, only to hit the IL due to lower back discomfort in September. The Dodgers think he's trending toward playing in the NLDS.
Does a Dodgers World Series guarantee a salary cap?
You'd think. Some certainly seem to think. However, let's take a view rooted not in optimism but in realism.
The owners want a salary cap. They wanted one before Shohei Ohtani signed on the dotted line of a $700 million contract. They wanted one before Shohei Ohtani was born (what else happened in 1994?). They want a salary cap for the same reason every owner in sports has wanted a salary cap — not for competitive balance but to remove pressure on them to spend like they want to compete.
The Dodgers have made for a convenient boogeyman by being baseball's biggest spender and baseball's best team over the past several years. They must be stopped to save baseball, or so the argument goes, as no team is supposed to have L.A.'s combination of resources, competence and aggression. It's just not fair. It almost goes without saying in many discussions that the point of a salary cap is to end the Dodgers' unfair dynasty.
And yet, it really needs to be noted: Commissioner Rob Manfred does not fantasize about the Dodgers being forced to dismantle their tremendous machine — of Andrew Friedman, on his knees, begging a small-market team to take Glasnow's contract off his books — like some salary-cap proponents seem to do. Ohtani winning rings on the Dodgers has worked out quite nicely for baseball. A salary cap can be introduced for cost control and the veneer of parity, but MLB ultimately benefits from the large-market teams being contenders with the biggest stars. As such, it's hard to imagine a salary cap being introduced in such a way that the Dodgers, Yankees, Mets and other top spenders are forced to take immediate action to get below a line. A slow introduction of a cap or some sort of contract grandfathering seems far more likely, giving the Dodgers and others time to adjust.
The Dodgers' recent success isn't so much fuel for a salary cap as it is fuel for salary-cap opinions. It has certainly convinced many fans of a salary cap's necessity, but the MLBPA is playing cards at a different table. They don't want a salary cap, no matter what the Dodgers do, and they and the MLB owners are ultimately the people whose opinions matter here.
Limitations on the Dodgers would merely be a byproduct of MLB getting what it wants, and that would be completely antithetical to the history of the union. It's difficult to imagine the next month impacting salary-cap discussions to any significant degree.
What about the money problems with Dodgers ownership?
That's still in progress, and it remains unclear how much it will affect the Dodgers.
The short version of a very complicated story is that the companies operated by Dodgers majority owner Mark Walter were found to be doing business with one another at a rate much greater than what they were telling customers, investors and regulators. Walter is now facing considerable legal scrutiny and has reacted by selling whatever he can to pay off some of the loans that turned out to be less than kosher.
His biggest move was to sell his majority stake in the Los Angeles Lakers at a franchise valuation of $12.5 billion, one year after buying the team at a $10 billion valuation. He has also offloaded his stake in the Premier League club Chelsea and the Ligue 1 club Strasbourg.
Those were big parts of Walter's sports portfolio, which also includes the WNBA's Los Angeles Sparks, the Cadillac Formula 1 team, the entire Professional Women's Hockey League and, of course, the Dodgers.
Dodgers leadership has repeatedly said the team isn't for sale. Of course, any sale would probably come out of nowhere — the Lakers' move was dropped on an otherwise uneventful Wednesday morning — but for now, that's mere speculation with the Dodgers.
One notable sign of trouble in Chavez Ravine, though, was a report that Walter recently approached Charter Communications about letting them out of their famously expensive Dodgers (and Lakers) contracts in exchange for a lump sum payout. It appears nothing has come out of that, but those are not stories you hear when everything is going well.
All of that's to say that Walter would likely welcome the immediate financial benefit of winning a third straight World Series even more than your typical billionaire. Of course, that outcome isn't up to him.

item.content:encoded:
While Francisco Lindor’s baseball career has made him one of the most recognizable players on the New York Mets, his life away from the diamond has become an equally important part of his public story. Puerto Rican shortstop reached another career milestone on September 27, 2026, hitting his 300th career home run against the Washington Nationals. The feat also made him just the 11th switch-hitter in MLB history to reach the 300 home run mark, and the second, behind Carlos Beltran, to combine that feat with at least 200 stolen bases.
Off the field, Lindor is married to his wife, Katia Reguero. The couple are proud parents of three children. The couple met on Instagram in 2020, before marrying in December 2021, and now share children Kalina Zoé, 3, and Amapola Chloé, 2, and son Koa Amani, 1. Reguero has also developed her own public persona through music, parenting talks and community work.
Francisco Lindor and Katia Reguero’s family life beyond Mets stardom
Francisco Lindor and Katia Reguero have raised a family and juggled the demanding schedule that comes with Major League Baseball. Lindor’s career involves plenty of travel, a long regular season and public scrutiny at all times, while Reguero has built her own professional and creative interests.
The couple have three children, Kalina Zoé born in November 2020, Amapola Chloé born in June 2023, and Koa Amani born in March 2025. Koa was born in the middle of the MLB season, and Lindor returned to the New York Mets shortly after his son’s birth. MLB said the Mets were preparing to play the Miami Marlins the following day, and Lindor was with the team.
Francisco Lindor and Katia Reguero’s marriage and children
Francisco Lindor and Katia Reguero's relationship began online in early 2020. Lindor messaged Reguero on Instagram, and they talked for about three months before meeting in person in Arizona. They ended up getting married, and their relationship blossomed as Lindor continued his baseball career.
The couple said "I do" on December 16, 2021, at Vizcaya Museum and Gardens in Miami, Florida. Their marriage came after they already had Kalina, giving the family a personal foundation before their wedding.
As Lindor’s career has progressed, so have family milestones. Lindor went back to be with Reguero when Koa was born in March 2025 and returned to the Mets. The moment illustrated how a player at the highest level can have family obligations and a demanding baseball schedule intersect.
Francisco Lindor and Katia Reguero’s lives beyond baseball
Lindor is more than his stats and his accomplishments with the New York Mets. His work with youth clinics, Boys & Girls Clubs and the Lindor Smiles community initiative is noted in MLB’s official profile, as well as a scholarship fund he created at Montverde Academy and a $1 million donation to the school’s Lindor Hall project.
Katia Reguero has also kept up interests outside of being Lindor’s wife. She has a background in music and has become known for her podcast and advocacy work in parenting. She also got noticed in 2026 playing the national anthem on violin at a New York Mets game, bringing another facet of her identity into the baseball environment around her family.
In September 2026, Lindor hit his 300th career home run, another milestone in his baseball career. Off the field, though, his life is one of marriage, three children, involvement in the community, and a wife who has built a public career in her own right. All of those factors combine to give a broader picture of the New York Mets star than just being an MLB shortstop.

item.content:encoded:
Published Oct 2, 2026 10:17 am
NEW YORK (AP) — Chicago Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong won the Baseball Digest major league player of the year award Friday, and Milwaukee Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski was selected pitcher of the year.
San Diego Padres closer Mason Miller was chosen reliever of the year.
Crow-Armstrong batted .280 with 45 home runs and 41 stolen bases this season, becoming the seventh member of the 40-40 club.
He led the majors in runs (119), tied for most homers, ranked second in OPS (.943) and finished fourth in RBIs (107). All while playing outstanding defense and appearing in all 162 regular-season games to help the Cubs earn a National League wild card.
The 24-year-old Crow-Armstrong received 21 of 24 first-place votes in balloting by a panel of baseball writers, broadcasters, reporters and researchers that included several former players, managers and executives.
Houston Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez finished second.
Crow-Armstrong became the seventh Cubs player to win the Baseball Digest award and first since Kris Bryant and Anthony Rizzo shared the prize in 2016.
The hard-throwing Misiorowski also garnered 21 first-place votes after going 16-5 to propel Milwaukee to the best record in the big leagues (103-59) and its fourth consecutive NL Central title. He led the majors with a 1.80 ERA and 252 strikeouts in 30 starts covering 174 2/3 innings.
New York Yankees right-hander Cam Schlittler was runner-up to the 24-year-old Misiorowski, the first Brewers pitcher to take home the honor.
Miller, 28, tied for the NL lead with a career-high 38 saves as the Padres earned a wild-card spot in the playoffs. He went 5-2 with a 1.67 ERA and 129 strikeouts in 70 innings over 66 appearances.
The right-hander received 18 first-place votes and easily outpaced Cleveland Guardians closer Cade Smith, who came in second.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Cubs Won't Get Into ‘Bidding War’ For Seiya Suzuki
item.dc:creator: Joey Pollizze
item.description: It didn't take long for free agent rumors to start swirling. The Chicago Cubs were just swept by the San Diego Padres in the National League Wild Card Round a few days ago, and free-agent rumors are already circling the baseball world. It will no doubt be a busy offseason for the Cubs, who have plenty of players hitting free agency. Players like Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga, David Peterson, and Carson Kelly will all test the open market this winter. However, the biggest question mark this offsea
item.content:encoded:
It didn't take long for free agent rumors to start swirling.
The Chicago Cubs were just swept by the San Diego Padres in the National League Wild Card Round a few days ago, and free-agent rumors are already circling the baseball world.
It will no doubt be a busy offseason for the Cubs, who have plenty of players hitting free agency. Players like Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga, David Peterson, and Carson Kelly will all test the open market this winter.
However, the biggest question mark this offseason for the Cubs is what they plan to do with their outfield. Both Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki are free agents at the conclusion of this year's World Series. That leaves the team in a potential rough spot.
The Cubs have to answer one of these questions ahead of free agency:
- Do we bring back both Happ and Suzuki and simply run it back with the same outfield core?
- Do we pay Happ and let Suzuki walk, since he will cost much less?
- Do we pay Suzuki big money and let Happ walk because Suzuki gives us the best chance to win?
The front office will obviously weigh all these options ahead of free agency. However, it seems as if the Cubs have already made somewhat of a decision about Suzuki's future with the organization.
Patrick Mooney of The Athletic reported that "it's unlikely that the Cubs will get into a bidding war for Suzuki's services, let alone win one."
Hearing that the Cubs won't enter a bidding war for Suzuki doesn't bode well for their chances of getting him back. Teams like the Dodgers, Blue Jays, and Yankees are better suited to get into a bidding war for the slugger than the North Siders.
Mitch Bannon of the Athletic already reported that the Blue Jays will pursue Suzuki this offseason. Given that Toronto isn't afraid to spend on big-time players (e.g., Dylan Cease last offseason), there's a strong chance that the outfielder doesn't re-sign with the Cubs.
Losing Suzuki in free agency would be a big loss for the North Siders. He has been one of the team's best power hitters since the Cubs signed him out of Japan in 2022. The Japanese slugger has 113 home runs over his five MLB seasons and has 58 home runs with 189 RBI combined over the past two years.
The Cubs would be losing that power bat at the top of their lineup if he goes to another team. Unfortunately, it's very possible he does leave.

item.title: [Diario AS] Dodgers NLDS roster: Who will make the 26-man playoff roster against the Braves?
item.dc:creator: Rodrigo Serrano; Jennifer Bubel
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers have won the National League West for the fifth consecutive season and for the 13th time in the last 14 years. The only team to interrupt their run was the San Francisco Giants in 2021. Since then, no one has been able to take the division away from Los Angeles. Now the defending back-to-back World Series champions are preparing for the National League Division Series, where they will face the Atlanta Braves beginning Saturday at Dodger Stadium. Atlanta advanced by defeat
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have won the National League West for the fifth consecutive season and for the 13th time in the last 14 years. The only team to interrupt their run was the San Francisco Giants in 2021. Since then, no one has been able to take the division away from Los Angeles.
Now the defending back-to-back World Series champions are preparing for the National League Division Series, where they will face the Atlanta Braves beginning Saturday at Dodger Stadium. Atlanta advanced by defeating the Philadelphia Phillies in the Wild Card Series, setting up the Dodgers’ first postseason matchup with the Braves since the 2021 NL Championship Series.
Your 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers. pic.twitter.com/XYs9LzjRIb
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 24, 2026
The Dodgers’ five-day bye gave Dave Roberts and his staff time to prepare their roster, and while most of the pieces are already in place, there are still some important decisions to make before the 26-man NLDS roster is finalized. MLB reports that the final bench spot remains particularly unsettled, while the bullpen could also have an opening depending on the health of Edgardo Henriquez.
Who will make the Dodgers’ pitching staff?
The Dodgers’ biggest strength heading into October is their starting rotation. Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, and Tyler Glasnow form a formidable group, although Roberts had not formally announced the order entering Friday.
Yamamoto is the leading candidate to start Game 1 against Atlanta. His normal rest schedule is one of the reasons the Japanese right-hander makes the most sense for the opener, as starting Saturday would also give him the chance to be available for a potential Game 5 on his usual rest.
#ITFDB presented by Toyo Tires. pic.twitter.com/TcKpliJrnR
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 24, 2026
The Dodgers also have several pitchers who could be used in relief despite spending much of the regular season as starters. Roki Sasaki, Justin Wrobleski and Emmet Sheehan are among the options who could give Roberts additional flexibility out of the bullpen.
Edgardo Henriquez is another name to watch. The right-hander emerged as an important leverage option during the regular season before lower back discomfort ended his year prematurely. The Dodgers planned to have him face hitters during the bye, with an activation for the NLDS possible if he comes through the workout without any problems.
What will the Dodgers’ offense look like?
Shohei Ohtani will once again be the centerpiece of the Dodgers’ offense, but the situation is different from what it appeared to be when the original story was written.
Ohtani returned from the injured list in late September and played in each of the Dodgers’ final five regular-season games. He went 5-for-21 with eight strikeouts and one walk during that stretch, but Roberts said the team had no health concerns with its superstar heading into the postseason.
It’s Shotime! On this day in 2024, Shohei Ohtani started the 50/50 club.
This MomenTito’s in Dodger history presented by Tito's Handmade Vodka. pic.twitter.com/cxOEcJyPNK
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 19, 2026
Ohtani is expected to remain the designated hitter, with Mookie Betts at shortstop, Freddie Freeman at first base and Max Muncy at third. The Dodgers’ outfield is also largely established, with Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages expected to occupy the three spots.
The lineup could continue to feature some adjustments depending on the opposing starter. Against right-handed pitching, Ohtani has been used at the top of the order, while Betts has taken the leadoff spot against left-handers. That platoon is expected to continue into October.
Who's your Player of the Game? Comment your answer below! pic.twitter.com/tt6sVtGvWT
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 26, 2026
Who gets the final roster spot?
The Dodgers have several candidates competing for what could be their final bench spot: Josue De Paula, Dalton Rushing, Alex Call, and Hyeseong Kim. MLB’s postseason preview identified the decision as one of the biggest remaining questions for the club.
De Paula is intriguing after his impressive first taste of the Majors. The Dodgers’ top prospect hit .323 with seven RBIs and seven runs scored in 11 games before being optioned to Triple-A when Ohtani returned from the injured list. His performance was strong enough to keep him in the postseason conversation.
But Kim offers something different. His defensive versatility, speed, and ability to contribute off the bench could make him valuable in a playoff series, particularly if Roberts wants another defensive option late in games.
MLB.com Dodgers beat reporter Sonja Chen noted that both De Paula and Kim could have a chance to make the NLDS roster if Los Angeles carries 14 position players and 12 pitchers. The final decision could ultimately come down to whether the Dodgers prefer another impact bat or additional speed and defense.
Rushing and Call remain possibilities as well, meaning the Dodgers have not simply decided between De Paula and Kim.
The other variable is the pitching staff. If Los Angeles carries only 12 pitchers rather than the maximum 13, it would open another position-player spot and potentially allow Roberts to keep more of those candidates.
Dodgers are chasing history
There is plenty more than a division title at stake for Los Angeles. The Dodgers are attempting to become the first team since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 to win three consecutive World Series titles. They have already won three of the past six championships and enter October as the defending champions for the second straight year.
Their first obstacle is now set: the Atlanta Braves. The two teams will meet Saturday in Game 1 of the NLDS at Dodger Stadium, with Yamamoto the likely starter for Los Angeles. Before the first pitch, however, Roberts and the Dodgers still have a handful of decisions to make about exactly which players will be part of their attempt at a historic three-peat.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Jacob Misiorowski vs. Padres: How Brewers Have Early NLDS Advantage
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy
item.description: After a few long days of waiting, we're finally just one day away from the Milwaukee Brewers kicking off their 2026 playoff run. Milwaukee will take the field on Saturday night against the San Diego Padres at American Family Field in Game 1 of the National League Division Series. It's been a long road to get here, but the playoffs have arrived and unsurprisingly, the first pitch of the postseason for Milwaukee will be from Jacob Misiorowski. The righty flamethrower was the best pitcher in baseba
item.content:encoded:
After a few long days of waiting, we're finally just one day away from the Milwaukee Brewers kicking off their 2026 playoff run.
Milwaukee will take the field on Saturday night against the San Diego Padres at American Family Field in Game 1 of the National League Division Series. It's been a long road to get here, but the playoffs have arrived and unsurprisingly, the first pitch of the postseason for Milwaukee will be from Jacob Misiorowski.
The righty flamethrower was the best pitcher in baseball throughout the 2026 season and he will have a chance to give Milwaukee an early lead in the series. The Padres aren't an easy matchup, to say the least. Fortunately, Misiorowski has already had some success against San Diego this season.
Misiorowski made a start against the Padres back on May 13. That day, the big righty tossed seven shutout innings and allowed just four base hits while striking out 10 batters. While that stat line is a bit absurd, it's pretty much in line with what he did all season to this point.
Jacob Misiorowski Give Milwaukee An Advantage
Misiorowski was the best pitcher in the league. There's no denying that fact. He finished the regular season with a league-leading 1.80 ERA to go along with 252 strikeouts in 174 2/3 innings pitched. The most earned runs he allowed in a game was five on Sep. 2. That was the only game in which he allowed more than three runs in a game all season. Simply put, he gave Milwaukee a chance to win every single time he touched the mound.
So, when it comes to Game 1, that's the guy you want to roll with. He was the best pitcher in baseball all season in general, plus he had individual success against the Padres. What else could you ask for?
Last season, the big flamethrower made three postseason appearances and had a 1.50 ERA in 12 innings of work. That was after struggling down the stretch and having his role shifted a bit with the organization. In the offseason, he went back to the lab and made a leap ahead of the 2026 season. If he pitches as he has all season to this point, Milwaukee should be able to come out on top in the first game of the five-game series. That's critical. Whoever wins Game 1 has a significant advantage the rest of the way in the series.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. item.content:encoded:
Ranking Phillies 2B Luis Arraez's Top 5 Landing Spots Ahead of MLB Free Agency
Any club pursuing three-time batting champion Luis Arraez will likely need a plan to play him regularly at second base.
In a 2026 season split between the San Francisco Giants and Philadelphia Phillies, Arraez returned to his natural position of second base. In terms of outs above average, he had the best season of his career, with San Francisco infield coach Ron Washington credited with helping his defensive growth.
Arraez should do better this offseason than the one-year, $12 million deal he settled for last offseason. He was unavailable for the Phillies' Wild Card Series loss to Atlanta because of a sprained left ankle, though the injury is not expected to affect his availability for 2027.
Let's take a look at the best potential landing spots for the four-time All-Star.
5. Texas Rangers
1 of 5
Whether the Rangers are in on Arraez will depend on whether managing partner Ray Davis authorizes president of baseball operations Chris Young to add payroll in the offseason.
From a baseball perspective, the Rangers' second basemen posted an OPS south of .700 this season. Clearly, Arraez would give them more offensively than they got in 2026.
Top prospect Sebastian Walcott is a shortstop/third baseman who is expected to play a role for the team in 2027. But even with Corey Seager at shortstop and Josh Jung at third base, Walcott seems more likely to play outfield than second base. There aren't many 6'4" second basemen.
4. Philadelphia Phillies
2 of 5
Arraez didn't perform as well with the Phillies as he did with the Giants, but his track record suggests that over a larger sample size, he will hit for a higher average.
The Phillies dealt pitching prospects Ramon Marquez and Marty Gair to acquire Arraez and reliever Caleb Kilian, so they should at least consider a reunion in free agency.
That said, some of this will come down to how the Phillies want to set up their infield in 2027. Alec Bohm will likely depart in free agency, while Bryce Harper is expected to return to first base.
Will the Phillies move Trea Turner off of shortstop, and if so will that be to second base or left field? What about Bryson Stott, whom the team likes at second base but moved to third to accommodate Arraez? Also looming is top prospect Aidan Miller, who missed most of 2026 but is an exciting bat who can play shortstop or third base.
Many moving parts make it unclear whether the Phillies will commit to multiple seasons of Arraez at second base. Still, his presence behind Bryce Harper gave Philadelphia a contact-oriented option in the heart of its lineup and may have made it easier for Harper to remain selective at the plate.
3. Pittsburgh Pirates
3 of 5
Will the Pirates extend the qualifying offer to Brandon Lowe? It's always difficult to know how owner Bob Nutting will operate. Even if the QO goes to Lowe, one would think he'd decline it in search of a multi-year commitment.
If Lowe ends up not returning to Pittsburgh, the Buccos will have a hole at second base. One way to soften the negative reaction to not bringing Lowe back after an excellent contract year is to sign a replacement as accomplished as Arraez.
You could do worse than a middle-infield pairing of Arraez and Konnor Griffin, especially in terms of offensive production.
2. San Francisco Giants
4 of 5
It's rare but not unheard of for a player to get traded midseason and then return to the club that traded him in the offseason as a free agent. This might be one of the instances where it makes sense, though.
Arraez not only built a great relationship with the aforementioned Washington, but he also hit .324 in 105 games with the Giants. While home run hitters other than Barry Bonds don't love Oracle Park, Arraez's offensive profile fit the park well. In 49 games at Oracle Park in 2026, Arraez hit .361.
This may come down to whether the Giants are comfortable with Casey Schmitt playing elsewhere on the diamond so Arraez can resume as the team's second baseman. Offensively, Arraez remains a great fit for the Giants.
1. Detroit Tigers
5 of 5
The Tigers will have quite a bit of money coming off the books this offseason, including the $22.025 million that Gleyber Torres made after accepting the qualifying offer last winter.
Arraez spent the first four seasons of his career with the Minnesota Twins, so a return to the AL Central could make sense. It's a bit surprising that Arraez has hit only .265 in 88 career plate appearances at Comerica Park, but the spacious outfield suits a contact hitter.
Additionally, with Torres coming off the books, the Tigers will have an opening at second base. Adding Arraez's bat-to-ball skills could help Detroit rebound from a disappointing 2026.

item.title: [FanSided] MLB Power Rankings: Every remaining playoff team after Wild Card Round
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline
item.description: With the exception of Braves-Phillies (of course), this year's Wild Card round was pretty lopsided. The competition should heat up in the Divisional Series, however. Not only are the best teams in each league being reintroduced, but we have division rivals and compelling stylistic contrasts. The Brewers and Padres could not be more different in how their teams were built. The Rays and Yankees don't like each other. The Guardians and White Sox also don't like each other. As for Braves-Dodgers? We
item.content:encoded:
With the exception of Braves-Phillies (of course), this year's Wild Card round was pretty lopsided. The competition should heat up in the Divisional Series, however. Not only are the best teams in each league being reintroduced, but we have division rivals and compelling stylistic contrasts.
The Brewers and Padres could not be more different in how their teams were built. The Rays and Yankees don't like each other. The Guardians and White Sox also don't like each other. As for Braves-Dodgers? Well, there's plenty of recent history there. But which teams have the look of title contenders as we move deeper into October? Let's rank all eight remaining teams in terms of championship equity.
8. Chicago White Sox
The White Sox made it hard on themselves down the stretch, but Chicago is riding high after a first-round sweep of the Astros, with blessings from the Pope. Coming into the postseason, the White Sox were broadly dinged for their youth and inexperience. As fate would have it, though, the South Siders were significantly more poised than a seasoned Astros team.
Chicago's lineup performed top to bottom. They worked deep into counts and made smart, situational swings. The rotation is still a mess, and the bullpen is not much better, but there's a lovable underdog quality to this White Sox team that is hard to ignore. By default, the White Sox rank last here, but an ALDS matchup with the Guardians is perfectly winnable. Do not discount the possibility of a South Siders pennant run.
7. Cleveland Guardians
Cleveland has been there and done that. This team is always the AL Central champ, it feels like, even when the odds are stacked against them. The Guardians hit much better down the stretch after a brutal start to the campaign, while their pitching is a potential superpower. Parker Messick and Gavin Williams can match just about any aces blow-for-blow, and this bullpen always tends to perform.
The question now becomes: Can Stephen Vogt's squad translate their signature Guards Ball style to October? The answer for years now has been "no." Cleveland lacks thump in the heart of the order, but tends to execute the small things — bunts, base-running, two-strike hitting — better than anyone. Chicago's pitching staff is vulnerable and the Guardians have the edge in experience, but so did Houston. And the Astros' bats were much better. The outcome of this series will not shock me in either direction, to be frank.
6. Atlanta Braves
The Braves lineup struggled down the stretch but appeared to wake up against the Phillies, especially in the clincher. Atlanta has no shortage of offensive talent and a deep bullpen, with plenty of postseason experience to draw on. So why ranked so low?
Well, the rotation is a mess. Chris Sale is an elite 1A, but Tyler Mahle is questionable against better offensive teams (see: Dodgers) and their third starter is Grant Holmes behind an opener. Atlanta has seven starters on the IL and could struggle to build a bridge to the stellar back end of their bullpen in non-Sale starts. That said, if the Braves' bats heat up, perhaps it does not matter. There is a clear break in quality between Cleveland at No. 7 and the rest of the field. The Braves are very, very capable of mounting a deep run. Atlanta notably went 5-1 against the Dodgers this season.
5. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays just kept winning all season long. There was no more consistent force in the American League. We can quibble with the back half of their lineup and question the depth of their rotation, but the Rays are an extremely disciplined club with star power (Junior Caminero) and fundamental skills (Chandler Simpson, Jonny DeLuca) in equal measure.
Tampa is going to defend at a high level and run the bases with intent. Their pitching staff does not look so fearsome on paper, but Drew Rasmussen is a bonafide ace and Freddy Peralta looked more like himself in September. Whether this team can match the raw explosiveness of the Yankees' lineup is the swing factor. On the flip side, New York has a propensity for unforced errors that Tampa can ruthlessly capitalize on.
4. New York Yankees
The Yankees are still waiting on Aaron Judge. New York stuffed its Wild Card roster with platoon bats and situational hitters, but Aaron Boone probably needs more pitchers for a five-game Divisional Series. The lineup exploded against the Red Sox, but Tampa will almost certainly manage its pitching staff better than Chad Tracy and Boston did.
New York is the best team in the American League on paper, even with all their injuries, but the bullpen is perilously thin and it's hard to trust this lineup completely. Ben Rice has caught fire at an optimal moment, so there's that. And the Yankees boast, by far, the most star power of any team west of Los Angeles. Whether it can all come together against a healthy, well-rested Rays team remains to be seen.
3. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers, almost without fail, dominate the regular season despite ownership's pervasive cheapness. This team knows how to develop talent in-house and locate value on the margins. There is no better-run small-market clubhouse in MLB. And yet, Milwaukee has consistently fallen flat in the playoffs. Whether or not this year is any different comes down to a couple factors.
First, Jacob Misiorowski helps. Milwaukee has the best pitcher in baseball and he may damn near guarantee a Game 1 win in the NLDS. The Brewers' bullpen is rock solid, too, while the depth of their rotation is respectable. Milwaukee's pitching can win ballgames. More importantly, there's less elite competition than usual; even the Dodgers are scuttling at the plate, while the entire American League is poked full of holes. The path has never been clearer for the Brewers, who compensate for limited slug with impressive plate discipline and savvy situational hitting. If Milwaukee can maintain its extraordinarily high baseline, there's reason to believe this could be the year it all clicks.
2. San Diego Padres
There are few stars I trust more in a high-leverage spot than Fernando Tatis Jr. The man just makes good things happen, whether he's using his power or his speed. San Diego's entire lineup, really, has come on strong in the final month. After sputtering for much of the regular season, the likes of Jackson Merrill and Manny Machado have apparently remembered how talented they are. Gavin Sheets and Ty France are improbably major contributors. On the pitching front, Michael King and Nick Pivetta tore through a loaded Cubs lineup. The Padres' bullpen is the best in baseball, so no team can more easily build a bridge between their frontline starters and the ninth inning.
San Diego's rotation depth is suspect; once Walker Buehler and Robbie Ray are asked to carry several innings, it could get dicey. But in terms of momentum and top shelf star power, the Padres clear the majority of the competition around them. It can't hurt that San Diego plays the Dodgers as well as any team, either. That matchup could ultimately define the 2026 season, assuming the Padres can out-slug the No. 1 seed Brewers.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
This shouldn't come as a shock. The Dodgers aren't as untouchable as their reputation suggests, but there's still only one team with Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow lined up on the mound. Meanwhile, Shohei Ohtani has proven his capacity for clutch swings time after time since arriving in Hollywood two years ago. Los Angeles has the best pitchers and the best player in MLB, with a star-studded lineup to boot. Mookie Betts, Kyle Tucker and Freddie Freeman weren't at the peak of their powers this season, but that's still a group worth trusting when every at-bat is magnified.
Los Angeles has depth, too. Josue De Paula is one of the most exciting young bats in baseball and the Dodgers barely have room for him on the roster. Alex Call and Dalton Rushing are useful as situational hitters. The primary concern is L.A.'s bullpen, but Rōki Sasaki, Kris Bubic and Justin Wrobleski — their excess rotation arms — should help the Dodgers cover innings when needed. The Dodgers are banged-up and very much vulnerable, but this is still the team to beat, full stop.

item.title: [si.com] Unlikely Hero Ray Kerr Silences Phillies As Braves Advance to NLDS
item.dc:creator: Ryan Phillips
item.description: The Braves powered their way to an NLDS berth after taking out their division rivals. On Thursday night, Atlanta won a winner-take-all Game 3 against the Phillies, 6–2, in front of a loud Truist Park crowd. The Braves tagged Philadelphia starter Aaron Nola for three runs in the bottom of the first inning and never looked back, leading wire-to-wire to eliminate their NL East peers. item.content:encoded:
The Braves powered their way to an NLDS berth after taking out their division rivals.
On Thursday night, Atlanta won a winner-take-all Game 3 against the Phillies, 6–2, in front of a loud Truist Park crowd. The Braves tagged Philadelphia starter Aaron Nola for three runs in the bottom of the first inning and never looked back, leading wire-to-wire to eliminate their NL East peers.
Surprise starter Ray Kerr, a 32-year-old with 72 2/3 career MLB innings, pitched into the fourth inning unscathed to keep the Phillies at arm’s length. The Phillies never found much offense beyond contributions from stars Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber, as the supporting cast beyond Alec Bohm failed to step up.
The victory sends Atlanta to Los Angeles for an NLDS matchup with the Dodgers starting on Saturday. For Philadelphia, a season that began with World Series ambitions was cut short in the wild-card round.
Here are our three takeaways from Game 3.
Braves Slug Their Way to NLDS
Atlanta relied heavily on the long ball in 2026, and with its season on the line that’s what it used to punch a ticket to the NLDS.
The Braves’ 204 regular season home runs ranked seventh in baseball, while their collective .409 slugging percentage was sixth. In Game 3, they flexed those muscles, blasting three home runs that accounted for each of their six runs.
Michael Harris II got things started in the bottom of the first, when he stepped to the plate with one out after back-to-back walks to Ronald Acuña Jr. and Matt Olson. He hammered a 2–0 sinker from Aaron Nola just over the right field wall to give Atlanta a 3–0 lead it wouldn’t relinquish.
Ozzie Albies got into the act three innings later when he launched a 96 mph four-seamer from Zack Wheeler 419 feet into the stands in right-center to increase the lead to 5–0.
Matt Olson added another in the seventh inning when he crushed a Jonathan Bowlan changeup to center to give Atlanta a 6–1 margin.
If the Braves are going to make a deep run in the playoffs, they’ll need to keep thumping baseballs out of the park. It’s the way they have played all year and it's how they were able to close out the Phillies.
The Ray Kerr Game
When the Braves announced their Game 3 starter, the collective response from the baseball world was: “Who?” We all know his name now.
Kerr had a remarkable path to signing with the Mariners as an undrafted free agent in 2017, at different points working at a movie theater and a 7-Eleven after dropping out of junior college. He bounced around the minors for several years and finally made his big league debut for the Padres at 27 years old in ’22, then recorded a 5.06 ERA in 29 games (32 innings) out of the bullpen over two seasons. He was then traded to Atlanta and recorded a 5.64 ERA in 10 games for Atlanta in 2024, but didn’t get back to the majors until Aug. 17 of this year. Once he did, he shined.
In nine appearances, he was 1–0 with a 1.47 ERA and a 0.60 WHIP. Still, he had three career starts entering Thursday night, and his team had never won any of them. The 32-year-old lefty made Atlanta manager Walt Weiss look like a genius Thursday night.
In his postseason debut, Kerr was locked in on the mound as he carved through a Phillies lineup loaded with All-Stars. He pitched 3 ⅓ shutout innings, allowing one hit, one walk and striking out two. Kerr left the game with a 3–0 lead. Atlanta’s rotation is banged up right now and they needed a big performance from whoever started Game 3. They got it from the last guy anyone expected.
Schwarber, Harper Get No Help
Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper brought the Phillies back from the dead in Game 2, hammering back-to-back home runs in the eighth inning to tie a game Philadelphia ultimately won in 10 innings. On Thursday night in Game 3, the duo combined to go 3-for-7 with a walk and a run scored. The rest of the lineup went 3-for-24 with two walks and a run. That wasn’t going to get it done.
As a team, the Phillies slashed .231/.270/.394 with 23 strikeouts over the three games, while Trea Turner went 1-for-11, Bryson Stott was 2-for-13 and J.T. Realmuto was 2-for-10. Alec Bohm was the only other hitter who showed up, going 4-for-12 with a home run. The offense that ranked 28th in wRC+ (92) during the regular season didn’t give enough support to its two main contributors, as the flaws that dogged the Phillies all year were predictably their undoing as they exited the postseason with a whimper.
If Philadelphia is going to keep its title window open, Schwarber and Harper need some help.
Ryan Phillips is a senior writer on the Breaking and Trending News team at Sports Illustrated. He has worked in digital media since 2009, spending eight years at The Big Lead before joining SI in 2024. Phillips also co-hosts The Assembly Call Podcast about Indiana Hoosiers basketball and previously worked at Bleacher Report. He is a proud San Diego native and a graduate of Indiana University’s journalism program.

item.title: [onpattison.com] Figuring out how to fix Trea Turner should be priority No. 1 for Phillies this offseason
item.dc:creator: Tim Kelly
item.description: ATLANTA — The question of the cause of the Phillies year-over-year offensive decline had barely been finished being asked before Trea Turner had an answer. “Me,” he said without hesitation. “I mean, it’s pretty simple. When you hit first or second, you get a lot of at-bats, and I kinda get things going. So a lot of that is on me. item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA — The question of the cause of the Phillies year-over-year offensive decline had barely been finished being asked before Trea Turner had an answer.
“Me,” he said without hesitation. “I mean, it’s pretty simple. When you hit first or second, you get a lot of at-bats, and I kinda get things going. So a lot of that is on me. I think Kyle and Bryce did a good job, I scored a lot of runs, and that’s mostly because those two guys had good years. I think it starts with me and I take a lot of responsibility for that.”
Just about any way you slice it, it was a disastrous year for Turner. The season came to an end Thursday as the Phillies were eliminated by the Atlanta Braves in the NLWCS.
A year after winning the NL batting title by hitting .304, Turner finished the 2026 season with a lower on-base percentage (.297) than his batting average from the prior campaign. He did homer 19 times, but after posting a .798 OPS across his first three seasons with the Phillies, Turner finished 2026 with a .675 OPS.
Defensively, he had a major bounce back in 2025, posting two defensive runs saved, 16 outs above average and making just eight errors across 1,216 1/3 innings. In 2026, he made 21 errors, while finishing the season with minus-17 defensive runs saved and minus-eight outs above average.
President of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski did once trade Prince Fielder — just two seasons into a nine-year/$214 million contract — to the Texas Rangers for Ian Kinsler. Even though the Tigers had to send $30 million to Texas, it was one of the finest trades of Dombrowski’s career, as he offloaded a bad contract and acquired a tremendous player in the process. Perhaps Dombrowski could facilitate a similar deal this offseason, even if the Phillies don’t get nearly as much back for Turner, who is still owed more than $189 million over the next seven seasons. Of course, Turner would have to sign off on moving, as his deal includes a full no-trade clause.
Assuming Turner is back, the Phillies will have to decide whether they believe he can continue to play shortstop or not. If they believe the answer is no, the Phillies will have to A) decide what position on the field they want to move Turner to and B) sell him on the plan. Even if they can compel him to change positions, they will want him to be bought in on his new position, be it second base, left field or somewhere else.
The bigger issue wherever Turner plays defensively and hits in the lineup might be getting him back on track mentally. He’s a smart guy, one who likes to dig deep into things to try to get out of a slump. While admirable, perhaps that’s to his detriment. Turner will play next season at 34 years old, so he may not quite be at his peak athleticism anymore. But he’s still really capable in that department. The bigger issue this year, particularly in the field, seemed to be his ability to actually make the play when he put himself in position to do so. Figuring out how to help a guy mentally might be harder than teaching him a new position defensively.
Turner has been open this season about his underperformance in 2026. So what will he do this offseason to try to reset?
“That’s a good question,” Turner acknowledged. “I’ve got a lot of work to do. Kinda just go over everything and just figure out as much as I can, find answers, see what I did badly. But I feel like this year is the biggest question mark for me offensively in a long time. I gotta figure that out. I’m definitely gonna have a lot of work to do there, and I’ll do it.”

item.dc:creator: Matt Wadleigh
item.description: Chris Sale got things started for the Atlanta Braves by starting Game 1 against the Philadelphia Phillies in the wild-card round. Sale finished the series against the Phillies as well. The Braves won on Thursday night, 6-2, but it was Sale who pitched the final 1.1 innings for Atlanta to end the game and send them to the NLDS against the Los Angeles Dodgers. As it turns out, Sale is the first pitcher to throw both the first and last pitches for his team in a postseason series since 2018. The oth
item.content:encoded:
Chris Sale got things started for the Atlanta Braves by starting Game 1 against the Philadelphia Phillies in the wild-card round.
Sale finished the series against the Phillies as well.
The Braves won on Thursday night, 6-2, but it was Sale who pitched the final 1.1 innings for Atlanta to end the game and send them to the NLDS against the Los Angeles Dodgers.
As it turns out, Sale is the first pitcher to throw both the first and last pitches for his team in a postseason series since 2018. The other one to do it in 2018? It was Chris Sale himself, when he was with the Boston Red Sox.
Chris Sale of the @Braves is the first MLB pitcher to throw both the first and last pitches for his team in a postseason series since he himself did so in the 2018 World Series. pic.twitter.com/7esVOkXBlT
— OptaSTATS (@OptaSTATS) October 2, 2026
In 2018, Sale started Game 1 of the World Series against the Dodgers, although he went just four innings and allowed three runs as the Red Sox won 8-4.
Sale then pitched the final inning of Game 5 as the Red Sox won the World Series.
Here was the scene from Thursday night.
Chris Sale sends the @Braves to the NLDS! #CLINCHED
(MLB x @BudweiserUSA) pic.twitter.com/gaa66CiYCy
Exactly one week ago, the @RedSox finished their most dominant season. pic.twitter.com/nqYzeKI0LD
— MLB (@MLB) November 5, 2018
Braves manager Walt Weiss used a total of six pitchers on Thursday night in a win-or-go-home scenario, and Sale threw 21 pitches to keep Atlanta's season alive.
The Braves face the Dodgers on Saturday in Game 1 and Sunday in Game 2, and it will be interesting to see when Sale gets his next start.

item.title: [MLB.com] Sale's pitch to Weiss pays off: Lefty bookends Braves' Wild Card Series win
item.dc:creator: Paul Casella
item.description: The Braves' ace had an important matter to address before Game 3 of the National League Wild Card Series on Thursday night at Truist Park. "First of all, I was not going to go to Chris Sale and ask him if he could pitch tonight," Weiss said after the Braves’ series-clinching 6-2 win. "I didn't want to put him in that position, because I knew that, even if he was hanging, he would tell me yes. So I was not going to bring it up." Turns out, Weiss didn't need to. "Literally as soon as I stepped in
item.content:encoded:
The Braves' ace had an important matter to address before Game 3 of the National League Wild Card Series on Thursday night at Truist Park.
"First of all, I was not going to go to Chris Sale and ask him if he could pitch tonight," Weiss said after the Braves’ series-clinching 6-2 win. "I didn't want to put him in that position, because I knew that, even if he was hanging, he would tell me yes. So I was not going to bring it up."
Turns out, Weiss didn't need to.
"Literally as soon as I stepped in my office this afternoon, he was sitting in the chair across from my desk," Weiss said. "And he looked at me and he said, 'I feel amazing.'”
Weiss’ response?
“Well, let's talk."
From there, the two laid out a plan that ultimately saw Sale take down the final four outs of the Braves' first postseason series win since the 2021 World Series. Keep in mind, Sale also recorded the club's first 19 outs of this Wild Card Series as the Game 1 starter in Atlanta's 5-3 victory two days earlier.
In doing so, Sale became the first pitcher to start Game 1 of a postseason series and finish off that same series since ... Chris Sale. He previously did the same thing for the Red Sox in the 2018 World Series against the Dodgers.
Sale joined Clayton Kershaw as the only pitchers to accomplish the feat multiple times in postseason history.
"What a warrior, man," Weiss said. "This guy -- I've run out of superlatives for Chris Sale. Been talking about him all year. He's one of the best I've ever been around."
Even with Sale’s mid-afternoon ambush opening up some options for Weiss, their meticulously crafted plan only worked if all of the pieces fell into place.
Ray Kerr had to go out and do his job as the opener. Grant Holmes had to take it from there and relay the torch to a trio of relievers -- Robert Suarez, Didier Fuentes and Dylan Dodd -- who each had to take care of business.
And even then, the offense also needed to do its part. Michael Harris II checked that box early with a three-run homer in the first inning, then Ozzie Albies (a two-run shot in the fourth) and Matt Olson (a solo blast in the seventh) tacked on.
"Unbelievable. I'm just thankful for the opportunity, honestly," Sale said. "This could not be more of a group effort. This was basically a culmination of our entire year. All hands on deck. Everyone is doing everything they can to just get a win for this team."
Safe to say everything went to plan?
Well, sort of.
Knowing the plan was to pitch against the top of the Phillies' order in either the eighth or the ninth inning, Sale started to throw in the bullpen in the top of the seventh. But when Olson's homer extended the Braves' lead to 6-1 in the bottom of the seventh, it altered the strategy.
Even with Philadelphia's 9-1-2 hitters due up, Weiss instead went with the left-handed Dodd to start the eighth. He gave up a leadoff triple to pinch-hitter Derek Hill, who then scored on Trea Turner's sacrifice fly to cut the lead to four.
Needing to face at least three batters, Dodd had to stay in to face Kyle Schwarber -- the same guy who homered in the eighth inning off Dylan Lee one day earlier to trigger the Phillies' Game 2 comeback. Dodd was up to the task, though, getting MLB's regular-season home run leader to fly out for the second out.
Then, it was showtime: Sale vs. Bryce Harper.
"Electric," Harris said of the moment Sale emerged from the bullpen.
"The best," Albies said. "The minute I saw him getting warmed up, I said, 'He's definitely coming in. I love this.' The energy, the excitement there -- everybody was pumped that he came in the game."
Well, everyone except the Phillies.
Sale struck out Harper on four pitches, getting him to chase three sliders well out of the zone. The last one missed badly enough to go to the backstop, but catcher Drake Baldwin tracked it down to throw out Harper.
Now came another decision for Weiss: Let Sale go back out for the ninth or turn it over to closer Raisel Iglesias with a four-run lead?
With Iglesias warming just in case, the home crowd roared as Sale emerged from the dugout to trot back out for the ninth. Four batters later, the Braves had punched their ticket for an NLDS showdown with the Dodgers.
"Was hoping he only had to go one," Weiss said, "but he had to get to four outs."
All told, Sale -- the Braves' presumed starter for Sunday's Game 2 -- threw 21 pitches over 1 1/3 innings.
Is he still good to go for Sunday?
"I don't know. I have no idea," Weiss said. "We weren't even worried about that. It was just, 'Put this thing down and then we'll have those conversations later.' But yeah, we haven't even talked about that. It was all about tonight."
If Weiss has any doubts, he’ll certainly be getting another visit this weekend at Dodger Stadium.
"If I had to pitch tomorrow," Sale said, "I'd pitch tomorrow."

item.title: [Bozeman Daily Chronicle] Bryce Harper after Phillies' early playoff exit: 'You're here to win games, and we didn't'
item.dc:creator: BILL TROCCHI
item.description: ATLANTA (AP) — Bryce Harper doesn't play the shoulda, woulda, coulda game. The bottom line for the Philadelphia Phillies is they came up short in the postseason again. “You’re here to do business. You’re here to win games, and we didn’t do that,” Harper said in a subdued Phillies clubhouse Thursday night following their 6-2 loss to the Atlanta Braves in the deciding Game 3 of their National League Wild Card Series. item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA (AP) — Bryce Harper doesn't play the shoulda, woulda, coulda game.
The bottom line for the Philadelphia Phillies is they came up short in the postseason again.
“You’re here to do business. You’re here to win games, and we didn’t do that,” Harper said in a subdued Phillies clubhouse Thursday night following their 6-2 loss to the Atlanta Braves in the deciding Game 3 of their National League Wild Card Series.
There would be no excuses coming from the All-Star slugger about a September swoon that prevented the Phillies from lining up their pitching against Atlanta because it took until Game 162 to clinch a playoff spot.
Philadelphia forced Game 3 against the Braves with three dramatic solo home runs late in Game 2. But in the end, the Phillies fell into an early hole Thursday and were eliminated from the postseason for the fifth consecutive year as they chase their first World Series title since 2008.
“You’d love to be able to set your pitching up and them be rested and all that kind of stuff,” interim manager Don Mattingly said. “But that’s not the way it went. We had to fight to get ourselves in, and to do what we had to do to get in, we had to do what we had to do basically every game in the series.”
The Phillies' core of Harper, Kyle Schwarber, J.T. Realmuto, Zack Wheeler and Aaron Nola have made five straight playoff appearances and averaged 91 wins per year during that stretch. They have yet to win a championship and have been eliminated further and further from that goal each season since reaching the 2022 World Series.
The following season, Philadelphia exited in the National League Championship Series, and the next two years saw losses in the Division Series. A wild-card exit this season marks another step in the wrong direction.
“Obviously, we'd love to win a World Series with these guys. We’ve been together quite a while, and we've got a good clubhouse, and you know, good characters on this team,” Nola said. “We know what type of guys are in here. We know what type of players we have, and what we’re capable of. (We need to) kind of play good at the right time.”
The five-year run included two playoff series wins over the Braves. Philadelphia eliminated Atlanta in 2022 and 2023 despite the Braves winning the NL East in both seasons. That scenario was set up again this year, with the Braves earning home-field advantage in this series by virtue of another NL East title.
This time, however, Atlanta managed to get the big hits and the clutch pitching when it mattered most. Ray Kerr, in just his 10th appearance this year and first career postseason appearance, played the role of opener to perfection. He went 3 1/3 innings, giving up no runs, one walk and one hit to set up bulk reliever Grant Holmes.
Michael Harris II belted a three-run homer off Nola in the first, and the Phillies were looking up the rest of the night.
The Phillies were looking up at the rest of their division in April, but eventually righted the ship. Mattingly took over when Rob Thomson was fired on April 28 after a 9-18 start. The Phillies won eight of their next nine and reached .500 on May 16. A red-hot August put them in playoff position, but a postseason berth was not secured until the final game of the regular season.
Mattingly deflected questions about his future after the game.
“It’s not the time to talk about it. I’m comfortable with whatever they want to do,” he said. “Again, I want the best for the Phillies. I loved being in Philly this year. I actually like playing in that environment. I like the environment. It’s a rough environment, but it’s good. Again, I think you let the organization evaluate, talk about what they think moving forward, what they should do, and that dictates a lot of different things.”
As the clubhouse emptied out for the final time this season, Wheeler reflected on the journey the Phillies went on and the disappointing ending it delivered.
“It is tough. We spent a lot of time together. We see everybody’s ups and downs,” he said. “We see the good times and bad times people have throughout the season. We’re all brothers here, and we love to compete. So something like this happens, it’s tough.”

item.title: [nbcphiladelphia.com] Phillies' season ends with the pain of another early postseason knockout
item.dc:creator: Jim Salisbury
item.description: ATLANTA – While the Phillies tried to extend their season Thursday night against the Atlanta Braves at Truist Park, their Delta 757 charter sat 23 miles away at Hartsfield-Jackson International airport. A win would send the Phillies west, to Los Angeles and a second straight National League Division Series matchup with the Dodgers. A loss would send them home, to Philadelphia and another long, cold winter. It didn’t take long to figure out which way the Phillies would be heading. Aaron Nola was
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA – While the Phillies tried to extend their season Thursday night against the Atlanta Braves at Truist Park, their Delta 757 charter sat 23 miles away at Hartsfield-Jackson International airport.
A win would send the Phillies west, to Los Angeles and a second straight National League Division Series matchup with the Dodgers.
A loss would send them home, to Philadelphia and another long, cold winter.
It didn’t take long to figure out which way the Phillies would be heading. Aaron Nola was tagged for three runs in the first inning. The Phillies never recovered. Their season came to an end in a 6-2 loss to the Braves in Game 3 of the NL Wild Card Series.
For just the second time in franchise history, the Phillies qualified for the postseason for a fifth straight year, matching a team-high streak first reached from 2007 to 2011. The Phils won the World Series in 2008, but have not since. They made a surprising run to the World Series in 2022 but were beaten by the Houston Astros in six games. They were a win away from returning to the World Series in 2023 only to collapse and lose Games 6 and 7 of the NL Championship Series at home to Arizona. Since then, they have gone the wrong way, losing in the Division Series (their first round of play) in 2024 and 2025 and now in the Wild Card Series.
“It’s always frustrating,” Kyle Schwarber said in the quiet of the losing clubhouse. “From every postseason I’ve been in, it always hurts when you’re not the last team standing.
“It’s just as frustrating this year as it was last year and the year before that.”
Philadelphia Phillies
Complete coverage of the Fightin' Phils and their MLB rivals from NBC Sports Philadelphia.
As the October defeats have mounted, the team’s core group of high-priced veteran players has gotten older.
Schwarber, always the optimist, insisted that the team’s championship window is still wide open. So did J.T. Realmuto, saying, “There’s definitely the talent in this room to win. If you watched us play all year, no matter who we played, we weren’t outmatched. It’s about execution. It’s not about the age and the years. We know we still have the talent to win.”
Over on the other side of the clubhouse, Bryce Harper didn’t sound so sure.
He was asked what gives him faith that the team can still get to where it wants to go.
“Yeah, I don’t know,” he said. “It’s going to be a long offseason, obviously. I have trust in the organization and the people that are in charge. We’ll see where we go.”
Heading into the offseason, the Phils have many questions, first and foremost: Will Don Mattingly return as manager in 2027? He took over, with an interim tag, for Rob Thomson after the team got off to a 9-19 start in April.
The Phillies played .590 ball (79-55) under Mattingly, but president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski tried to hire Alex Cora when he let Thomson go, and he seems likely to try again in the coming weeks. Stay tuned.
Mattingly would not touch the topic after the game. Schwarber, Realmuto, Nola and Trea Turner all said they’d like to see Mattingly return. Harper declined to talk about the topic.
If Cora comes on board, he will be taking over a team of highs and lows, one with an inconsistent offense that is seemingly up one month (see August) and down the next (see September). He will be taking over a team that lacks pitching depth, both in the starting rotation and the bullpen. Both weaknesses reared their head in recent weeks as the Phils had to scramble to make the playoffs, using ace Zack Wheeler on the final day of the regular season, a circumstance that prevented him from starting Game 1 of the postseason.
Wheeler mentioned the team’s overall inconsistency when asked if he believed the Phils still had the talent to make a deeper postseason run next year.
“Consistency in every group, I think that’s what will get us there,” he said. “We were kind of inconsistent throughout the year. Maybe we were hitting, but we weren’t pitching well. Maybe we were pitching well and we weren’t hitting well. We just have to put it all together throughout the majority of the season.
“We’re hungry, that’s for sure. We just didn’t get the job done.”
The Phils had chances to win the series.
Jesus Luzardo pitched well in Game 1 and they held a 3-2 lead in the seventh. With few trusted arms in his leaky bullpen, Mattingly went to his All-Star closer, Jhoan Duran, in the bottom of the seventh. Duran got through that inning but gave up the lead on a three-run homer in the eighth and the Phillies lost, 5-3.
They bounced back to win a wild Game 2 Wednesday in 10 innings on the strength of three late home runs and the clutch pitching of Cristopher Sanchez, Alex McFarlane and Andrew Painter. They seemed to have momentum heading into Game 3.
But the momentum disappeared quickly as Nola had big trouble throwing strikes.
Just three of the right-hander's first 13 pitches to open the game were strikes. He fell behind Ronald Acuna Jr., and Matt Olson, the Braves’ Nos. 2 and 3 hitters, with 3-0 counts and eventually walked both. He then fell behind Michael Harris II, 2-0. Harris hit the next pitch, a sinker down and out of the zone, over the right-field wall for a three-run homer.
“I think he was just a little too careful,” Realmuto said of Nola. “I don’t think he was way off because he was just missing. They just did a good job of not chasing and making him come in the zone. When a lineup is good like that and they get on a roll, it’s tough to get them out when they’re not chasing.”
Nola did not make it through the second inning. Tim Mayza got the final out of the frame before handing off to Wheeler in the top of the third. The Phillies’ brain trust opted not to start Wheeler on three days’ rest. He'd never done that before. Also, Wheeler admitted that at this point of the season, he wasn’t feeling 100 percent. It was decided that Nola’s best chance of succeeding would be to stay in a starter’s role.
“We’re going to need Nola in this game,” Mattingly said before the game. “Starting him gives us the best version of him.”
The Phillies weren’t sure Wheeler would even be able to pitch until he tested himself by playing catch before the game. He ended up pitching four innings but was not particularly sharp. He gave up three hits and walked three. One of those walks turned into a run when Ozzie Albies stroked a two-run homer in the fourth to give the Braves a 5-0 lead.
“We felt Nola was on solid rest,” Mattingly said after the game. “If he could get us into the game at all, we’d have Zack after that. Obviously, it didn’t go well.”
Atlanta used lefty Ray Kerr as an opener. He pitched 3 1/3 innings and did not allow a run. The only hit Kerr gave up was a single to Schwarber in the first inning. Kerr then struck out Harper.
Grant Holmes, Robert Suarez, Didier Fuentes, Dylan Dodd and Chris Sale finished off the Phillies. Sale, the Braves’ ace lefty who started Game 1, entered with two outs in the eighth and struck out Harper.
Before the 2019 season, Harper signed a 13-year, $330-million contract with the Phillies. He came looking for a parade down Broad Street. Eight years later, he boarded a flight back to Philadelphia, still looking.
